If you terminate TLS at an ingress and use aws:SecureTransport, set --trusted-proxies; without it, every request counts as plain HTTP.

{"Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:GetObject",
 "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::partner-feed/*",
 "Condition": {"IpAddress": {"aws:SourceIp": "203.0.113.0/24"}}}

In Kubernetes, pod addresses change. To mean "inside the cluster", prefer endpoint names; keep IP conditions for fixed networks such as an office range or a partner's servers.

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
gateway:
  endpoints:
    internalName: internal        # the gateway Service
    external:
      port: 9010                  # a second port; the ingress targets it
      name: external
  trustedProxies: "10.244.0.0/16"

docs.title: Do I need a private endpoint?
docs.text:
Usually not. If the applications run in the same cluster as ObjectIO, the gateway's ClusterIP Service is already private: traffic stays in the cluster unless you also expose it through an ingress.

Block Public Access is about something else: who may read without credentials, not which network the request uses. Keep it on either way. Endpoint names connect the two when you want "anyone inside the cluster, but no one outside".

docs.title: Bucket replication
docs.text: Copy every new version written to a bucket into a bucket on another ObjectIO cluster, asynchronously, so losing a site loses nothing that had time to replicate.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. On the target cluster: a versioned bucket, and credentials for the source to write with. The admin's work; for least privilege, a user with s3:PutObject, s3:ReplicateObject (and s3:DeleteObject, s3:ReplicateDelete if delete markers replicate) on that bucket.

aws s3api create-bucket --bucket dr-copy --endpoint-url https://site-b:9000
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket dr-copy \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled --endpoint-url https://site-b:9000

2. On the source cluster: the target. Targets belong to a tenant: a bucket's rules can name only its own tenant's targets, so one tenant can never send data into another's remote bucket with the other's credentials. A tenant's admin manages its tenant's targets; the system admin manages the system's (no ?tenant=) and any tenant's (?tenant=).

curl -X POST https://site-a:9000/_admin/replication/targets \
  --aws-sigv4 aws:amz:us-east-1:s3 --user "$AK:$SK" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "site-b", "endpoint": "https://site-b:9000", "bucket": "dr-copy",
       "access_key": "...", "secret_key": "..."}'

GET /_admin/replication/targets lists a tenant's targets (the caller's own, for a tenant admin; secrets never shown); DELETE /_admin/replication/targets/{name} removes one. Both take ?tenant= for the system admin. The secret is kept in meta, as users' secret keys are.

A target a tenant's admin sets must be https://, on a host the operator allows tenants (as for tenant audit webhooks); otherwise a tenant could make the gateway send requests to addresses inside the cluster. Until the operator allows some, tenant admins can't set targets, and the system admin sets them with ?tenant=, unrestricted:

curl -X PUT https://site-a:9000/_admin/replication/settings \
  --aws-sigv4 aws:amz:us-east-1:s3 --user "$AK:$SK" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"allowed_tenant_hosts": ["dr.example.com", "*.dr.example.com"]}'

The list is checked again at every send, so removing a host stops tenants' targets on it.

3. On the source bucket: versioning, then the rules (S3's PutBucketReplication), by the bucket's owner or anyone its policy grants s3:PutReplicationConfiguration. The destination names one of the bucket's tenant's targets: arn:obio:replication:::<target>.

<ReplicationConfiguration>
  <Rule>
    <ID>everything</ID>
    <Status>Enabled</Status>
    <Filter><Prefix></Prefix></Filter>
    <DeleteMarkerReplication><Status>Disabled</Status></DeleteMarkerReplication>
    <Destination><Bucket>arn:obio:replication:::site-b</Bucket></Destination>
  </Rule>
</ReplicationConfiguration>

aws s3api put-bucket-replication --bucket photos \
  --replication-configuration file://rules.json --endpoint-url https://site-a:9000

A rule filters by prefix and tags (<And> for both). Both buckets must be versioned; the rules are refused otherwise.

docs.title: What replicates
docs.text:
Change on the source On the target A new version (PUT, multipart upload, copy) The same version: same version id, bytes, ETag, content headers, x-amz-meta-*, tags, Object Lock retention and legal hold, SSE-S3 / SSE-KMS encryption (re-encrypted with the target's keys; an SSE-KMS key id must exist there) A delete marker Only if the rule has DeleteMarkerReplication Enabled A DELETE of a specific version Never: a mistake or an attacker on one site can't destroy the other's copy An SSE-C object Not replicated (its key isn't ours to send), as in S3 Objects written before the rule Not yet (a resync is coming); copy them once with your usual tooling

The target never replicates a replica onward, so two clusters with rules pointing at each other don't loop.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A version a rule covers is committed with each target marked PENDING, in the same metadata write: no version is ever committed and forgotten.
  • The gateway that took the write sends it at once. One gateway at a time (a lease in meta) also scans every bucket with rules, every --replication-scan-secs (30 s by default), for versions still PENDING or FAILED, and sends them oldest first. That is what makes it reliable: after a crash, or while a target was down, every marked version is found.
  • A failed send is retried with backoff (2 s, doubling, up to 5 min), indefinitely. FAILED is a status to alert on, not a give-up.
  • Objects up to 64 MiB go in one PUT; larger ones as a multipart upload of 16 MiB parts.
  • The target stores a version it already holds (same version id and ETag) once: a send repeated after a crash changes nothing. An older version arriving after a newer one is kept as a version, never made current.

docs.title: Watching it
docs.text:
• x-amz-replication-status on HEAD and GET: PENDING, COMPLETED or FAILED on the source, REPLICA on the target.
  • Metrics (gateway /metrics):
  • objectio_replication_backlog{target}: versions not yet replicated, at the last scan;
  • objectio_replication_lag_seconds{target}: the oldest one's age, in effect the RPO;
  • objectio_replication_sent_total{target,result};
  • objectio_replication_bytes_total{target}.

Alert on lag that keeps growing, and on result="error".

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text: Existing-object resync, per-target bandwidth limits, and targets that aren't ObjectIO (AWS S3, MinIO) are the next phases.

docs.title: S3 API Operations
docs.text: Supported S3 API operations in ObjectIO.

docs.title: ListBuckets
docs.text:
List all buckets owned by the authenticated user.

GET /

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<ListAllMyBucketsResult>
    <Owner>
        <ID>user-id</ID>
        <DisplayName>User Name</DisplayName>
    </Owner>
    <Buckets>
        <Bucket>
            <Name>my-bucket</Name>
            <CreationDate>2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z</CreationDate>
        </Bucket>
    </Buckets>
</ListAllMyBucketsResult>

docs.title: CreateBucket
docs.text:
Create a new bucket.

PUT /{bucket}

Headers: - x-amz-acl: only private or bucket-owner-full-control (ACLs are owner-enforced) - x-amz-bucket-object-lock-enabled: true: a lock bucket (versioned) - x-objectio-pool: <pool>: the pool its data goes to (default: the tenant's default pool, else the cluster's default placement). A tenant may use only its default and allowed pools; the pool is fixed for the bucket's life

Response: 200 OK

A new bucket starts with public access blocked, and with no configuration from any earlier bucket of the same name.

docs.title: DeleteBucket
docs.text:
Delete an empty bucket.

DELETE /{bucket}

Response: 204 No Content

Errors: - BucketNotEmpty: the bucket holds objects, or (versioned) noncurrent versions or delete markers

Deleting a bucket also removes its policy, object lock, lifecycle, encryption and public access settings, in the same commit.

docs.title: HeadBucket
docs.text:
Check if a bucket exists and you have access.

HEAD /{bucket}

Response: 200 OK (bucket exists) or 404 Not Found

docs.title: GetBucketLocation
docs.text:
Get the region of a bucket.

GET /{bucket}?location

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<LocationConstraint>us-east-1</LocationConstraint>

docs.title: PutObject
docs.text:
Upload an object.

PUT /{bucket}/{key}

Headers: - Content-Type: MIME type - Content-Length: Object size - x-amz-meta-*: User metadata - Cache-Control, Content-Disposition, Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Expires: kept with the object and served back (and kept by a copy) - If-None-Match: *: write only if no object has the key (412 PreconditionFailed if one does) — a create that can't overwrite - If-Match: <etag>: write only if the current object has this ETag (412, or 404 NoSuchKey if there's none) — compare-and-swap

Conditional writes are checked and applied atomically: of two writers racing with If-None-Match: *, exactly one wins. CompleteMultipartUpload takes the same headers.

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e"

Example:

curl -X PUT \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
  -d "Hello World" \
  http://localhost:9000/my-bucket/hello.txt

docs.title: GetObject
docs.text:
Download an object.

GET /{bucket}/{key}

Headers: - Range: Byte range (optional)

Response Headers: - Content-Type: Object MIME type - Content-Length: Object size - ETag: Object hash - Last-Modified: Last modification time

Range Request:

curl -H "Range: bytes=0-99" http://localhost:9000/my-bucket/file.txt

docs.title: HeadObject
docs.text:
Get object metadata without body.

HEAD /{bucket}/{key}

Response Headers: - Content-Type: Object MIME type - Content-Length: Object size - ETag: Object hash - x-amz-meta-*: User metadata

docs.title: DeleteObject
docs.text:
Delete an object.

DELETE /{bucket}/{key}

Response: 204 No Content

docs.title: CopyObject
docs.text:
Copy an object.

PUT /{bucket}/{key}
x-amz-copy-source: /source-bucket/source-key

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<CopyObjectResult>
    <LastModified>2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z</LastModified>
    <ETag>"d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e"</ETag>
</CopyObjectResult>

docs.title: ListObjectsV2
docs.text:
List objects in a bucket.

GET /{bucket}?list-type=2

Parameters: - prefix: Filter by prefix - delimiter: Group by delimiter - max-keys: Max results (default: 1000) - continuation-token: Pagination token - start-after: Start listing after this key

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<ListBucketResult>
    <Name>my-bucket</Name>
    <Prefix></Prefix>
    <MaxKeys>1000</MaxKeys>
    <IsTruncated>false</IsTruncated>
    <Contents>
        <Key>file1.txt</Key>
        <LastModified>2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z</LastModified>
        <ETag>"abc123"</ETag>
        <Size>1024</Size>
        <StorageClass>STANDARD</StorageClass>
    </Contents>
</ListBucketResult>

docs.title: Multipart Upload
docs.text: Multipart upload allows uploading large objects in parts, which is required for files larger than 5GB and recommended for files larger than 100MB.

docs.title: Limits and Behavior
docs.text: Parameter Value Notes Minimum part size 5 MB Except last part Maximum part size 5 GB Maximum parts 10,000 Maximum object size 5 TB 10,000 × 5GB Default AWS CLI part size 8 MB Configurable via --multipart-chunk-size

docs.title: Multi-Stripe Chunking
docs.text:
ObjectIO uses a 4MB internal block size. When a part exceeds 4MB, it is automatically split into multiple stripes:

8 MB Part Upload:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   8 MB Part Data                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                         │
              Split into ~4MB stripes
                         │
         ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
         ▼                               ▼
    ┌─────────┐                     ┌─────────┐
    │ Stripe 0│ (4 MB)              │ Stripe 1│ (4 MB)
    └────┬────┘                     └────┬────┘
         │                               │
    EC Encode (4+2)                 EC Encode (4+2)
         │                               │
    6 shards                        6 shards

Each stripe is independently erasure-coded and distributed across storage nodes.

docs.title: CreateMultipartUpload
docs.text:
Initiate a multipart upload.

POST /{bucket}/{key}?uploads

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<InitiateMultipartUploadResult>
    <Bucket>my-bucket</Bucket>
    <Key>large-file.zip</Key>
    <UploadId>abc123</UploadId>
</InitiateMultipartUploadResult>

docs.title: UploadPart
docs.text:
Upload a part. Parts can be uploaded in any order and in parallel.

PUT /{bucket}/{key}?partNumber={n}&uploadId={id}

Parameters:

  • partNumber: 1 to 10,000
  • uploadId: From CreateMultipartUpload response

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "part-etag"

Example with curl:

# Upload part 1
curl -X PUT \
  "http://localhost:9000/my-bucket/large-file?partNumber=1&uploadId=abc123" \
  --data-binary @part1.bin

docs.title: CompleteMultipartUpload
docs.text:
Complete the upload by providing the list of parts in order.

POST /{bucket}/{key}?uploadId={id}

Request Body:

<CompleteMultipartUpload>
    <Part>
        <PartNumber>1</PartNumber>
        <ETag>"part1-etag"</ETag>
    </Part>
    <Part>
        <PartNumber>2</PartNumber>
        <ETag>"part2-etag"</ETag>
    </Part>
</CompleteMultipartUpload>

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<CompleteMultipartUploadResult>
    <Location>http://localhost:9000/my-bucket/large-file</Location>
    <Bucket>my-bucket</Bucket>
    <Key>large-file</Key>
    <ETag>"abc123-2"</ETag>
</CompleteMultipartUploadResult>

The final ETag format is "<md5-of-part-md5s>-<part-count>".

docs.title: AbortMultipartUpload
docs.text:
Abort an in-progress upload and delete uploaded parts.

DELETE /{bucket}/{key}?uploadId={id}

Response: 204 No Content

docs.title: ListParts
docs.text:
List uploaded parts for an in-progress multipart upload.

GET /{bucket}/{key}?uploadId={id}

Parameters:

  • max-parts: Maximum parts to return (default: 1000)
  • part-number-marker: Start listing after this part number

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<ListPartsResult>
    <Bucket>my-bucket</Bucket>
    <Key>large-file</Key>
    <UploadId>abc123</UploadId>
    <MaxParts>1000</MaxParts>
    <IsTruncated>false</IsTruncated>
    <Part>
        <PartNumber>1</PartNumber>
        <LastModified>2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z</LastModified>
        <ETag>"part1-etag"</ETag>
        <Size>8388608</Size>
    </Part>
</ListPartsResult>

docs.title: ListMultipartUploads
docs.text:
List in-progress multipart uploads for a bucket.

GET /{bucket}?uploads

Parameters:

  • prefix: Filter by key prefix
  • max-uploads: Maximum uploads to return (default: 1000)

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<ListMultipartUploadsResult>
    <Bucket>my-bucket</Bucket>
    <MaxUploads>1000</MaxUploads>
    <IsTruncated>false</IsTruncated>
    <Upload>
        <Key>large-file</Key>
        <UploadId>abc123</UploadId>
        <Initiated>2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z</Initiated>
    </Upload>
</ListMultipartUploadsResult>

docs.title: Example: Upload Large File with AWS CLI
docs.text:
# AWS CLI automatically uses multipart upload for files > 8MB
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 cp large-file.zip s3://my-bucket/

# Configure part size (minimum 5MB)
aws configure set default.s3.multipart_chunksize 16MB
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 cp large-file.zip s3://my-bucket/

# Manual multipart upload
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3api create-multipart-upload \
  --bucket my-bucket --key large-file.zip

# Upload parts
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3api upload-part \
  --bucket my-bucket --key large-file.zip \
  --part-number 1 --upload-id $UPLOAD_ID --body part1.bin

# Complete upload
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3api complete-multipart-upload \
  --bucket my-bucket --key large-file.zip \
  --upload-id $UPLOAD_ID \
  --multipart-upload file://parts.json

docs.title: PutBucketPolicy
docs.text:
Set bucket policy.

PUT /{bucket}?policy

Request Body:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": "*",
            "Action": "s3:GetObject",
            "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"
        }
    ]
}

docs.title: GetBucketPolicy
docs.text:
Get bucket policy.

GET /{bucket}?policy

docs.title: DeleteBucketPolicy
docs.text:
Delete bucket policy.

DELETE /{bucket}?policy

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
PUT    /{bucket}?lifecycle
GET    /{bucket}?lifecycle      → 404 NoSuchLifecycleConfiguration when none
DELETE /{bucket}?lifecycle

<LifecycleConfiguration>
  <Rule>
    <ID>logs</ID>
    <Filter><Prefix>logs/</Prefix></Filter>
    <Status>Enabled</Status>
    <Expiration><Days>30</Days></Expiration>
  </Rule>
  <Rule>
    <ID>old-versions</ID>
    <Filter/>
    <Status>Enabled</Status>
    <NoncurrentVersionExpiration>
      <NoncurrentDays>7</NoncurrentDays>
      <NewerNoncurrentVersions>3</NewerNoncurrentVersions>
    </NoncurrentVersionExpiration>
    <AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload><DaysAfterInitiation>2</DaysAfterInitiation></AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload>
  </Rule>
</LifecycleConfiguration>
action what happens Expiration Days / Date The current version expires. Unversioned: deleted. Versioned or suspended: a delete marker is added, as a DELETE without a version id would — the data stays as a noncurrent version. Expiration ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker A delete marker that is the key's only version is removed. Days does this too in a versioned bucket. A marker with versions behind it is never removed: that would bring the object back. NoncurrentVersionExpiration A noncurrent version is deleted once it has been noncurrent for NoncurrentDays (counted from when the next version was written), keeping the newest NewerNoncurrentVersions noncurrent versions whatever their age. AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload Uploads started more than DaysAfterInitiation days ago are aborted and their parts reclaimed.

Filters: <Prefix>, <Tag>, <ObjectSizeGreaterThan>, <ObjectSizeLessThan>, or several inside <And>; the legacy top-level <Prefix> is accepted. Tag and size filters don't apply to delete markers.

Guarantees. Lifecycle acts through the same delete path as a client, so a version under Object Lock retention or a legal hold is left alone (and counted in objectio_lifecycle_actions_total{action="locked"}), the listing stays right, and space is reclaimed. Every action is an audit event by principal lifecycle:<rule id>.

When. One gateway at a time scans (a lease held in meta); --lifecycle-interval-secs sets how often (default hourly). An object becomes eligible once its age passes the rule's days; it is acted on at the next scan.

Refused: Transition / NoncurrentVersionTransition (InvalidStorageClass — there is one storage class), Days ≤ 0, a Date not at midnight UTC, rules without an action, duplicate IDs, Filter and Prefix together.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
PUT    /{bucket}?cors
GET    /{bucket}?cors      → 404 NoSuchCORSConfiguration when none
DELETE /{bucket}?cors

<CORSConfiguration>
  <CORSRule>
    <ID>web-app</ID>
    <AllowedOrigin>https://app.example.com</AllowedOrigin>
    <AllowedOrigin>https://*.example.com</AllowedOrigin>
    <AllowedMethod>GET</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedMethod>PUT</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedHeader>*</AllowedHeader>
    <ExposeHeader>ETag</ExposeHeader>
    <MaxAgeSeconds>3000</MaxAgeSeconds>
  </CORSRule>
</CORSConfiguration>
  • Preflights (OPTIONS on a bucket or object) are answered without credentials — browsers never sign them — from the configuration alone: the first rule allowing the origin, the method and every requested header. No match (or no configuration): 403 AccessForbidden. A preflight reveals nothing but whether the bucket exists.
  • Actual requests with an Origin that a rule allows get Access-Control-Allow-Origin (the origin itself, with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, unless the rule's origin is exactly *), -Allow-Methods, -Expose-Headers, -Max-Age and Vary: Origin — error responses included, so a browser can read S3's errors. CORS only adds headers: every request is still authenticated and authorized.
  • Up to 100 rules; methods GET PUT POST DELETE HEAD; at most one * in an origin or header pattern.

docs.title: POST Object (browser uploads)
docs.text:
A browser uploads straight into a bucket with an HTML form, signed by your backend — the S3 form-upload API, so boto3's generate_presigned_post and every S3 form library work.

post = s3.generate_presigned_post(
    "uploads", "user-42/${filename}",
    Conditions=[["starts-with", "$key", "user-42/"], ["content-length-range", 1, 10_000_000]],
    ExpiresIn=600)
# hand post["url"] and post["fields"] to the browser's form
  • POST /{bucket} with multipart/form-data; fields key (with ${filename}), policy, x-amz-algorithm (AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 only), x-amz-credential, x-amz-date, x-amz-signature, optional x-amz-security-token, Content-Type, Cache-Control, Content-Disposition, x-amz-meta-*, success_action_status (200, 201, 204), success_action_redirect, and file last.
  • The policy must not have expired, and every form field (except the signature, file, policy and x-ignore-*) must be covered by one of its conditions: exact match, eq, starts-with, content-length-range. The signature and policy are checked before any of the file is read, and the file is read only up to the policy's size limit (and the single-PUT limit, 100 MiB).
  • Authorization is the signer's, exactly as for a PUT: scoped keys, the tenant boundary, policies and Block Public Access all apply. The object is written by the same path a PUT takes (default encryption, Object Lock, versioning, checksums).
  • A form without a signature is anonymous: it needs a bucket policy allowing anonymous s3:PutObject, and public access not blocked.
  • Responses: 204 by default, 200, 201 with a PostResponse document, or 303 to success_action_redirect. Policy violations: 403 AccessDenied ("Invalid according to Policy: …"); a file outside content-length-range: 400 EntityTooLarge / EntityTooSmall.

docs.title: Public Access Block
docs.text:
See Public Access for what the flags do and the tenant- and cluster-wide equivalents.

PUT /{bucket}?publicAccessBlock set the bucket's block (PublicAccessBlockConfiguration XML; absent flags are false) GET /{bucket}?publicAccessBlock the bucket's own block; 404 NoSuchPublicAccessBlockConfiguration if none DELETE /{bucket}?publicAccessBlock remove it (tenant and cluster blocks still apply) GET /{bucket}?policyStatus <PolicyStatus><IsPublic> — whether the bucket policy makes it public

PutBucketPolicy answers 403 AccessDenied for a public policy while BlockPublicPolicy holds at any level.

docs.title: ACLs
docs.text: Buckets are bucket owner enforced. GetBucketAcl / GetObjectAcl answer the owner with FULL_CONTROL; GetBucketOwnershipControls answers BucketOwnerEnforced. An ACL write naming only that is accepted; any other is 400 AccessControlListNotSupported. See ACLs.

docs.title: PutBucketVersioning
docs.text:
Enable/suspend versioning.

PUT /{bucket}?versioning

Request Body:

<VersioningConfiguration>
    <Status>Enabled</Status>
</VersioningConfiguration>

docs.title: GetBucketVersioning
docs.text:
Get versioning status.

GET /{bucket}?versioning

docs.title: ListObjectVersions
docs.text:
List object versions.

GET /{bucket}?versions

docs.title: Not Yet Implemented
docs.text:
A request naming one of these sub-resources is refused with 501 NotImplemented (rather than, say, GET /b?website listing the bucket). Bucket logging (?logging) is supported: see Bucket Logging.

  • S3 Select
  • Inventory, Analytics, Metrics configuration
  • Website configuration
  • Accelerate configuration, Request Payment
  • SigV2 — refused with 400; use SigV4

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Everything you need to stand up ObjectIO — from a one-binary demo on a laptop to a production Kubernetes install.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Path Walkthrough Best for 🚀 Fastest demo quickstart.md One binary or one container, <60 s to aws s3 ls 🐧 Bare-metal Linux linux.md Production servers, systemd, raw disks 🍏 macOS macos.md Dev laptops (AIO only — not a production target) 🐳 Docker & Compose docker.md Local clusters, CI, single-host appliances ☸ Kubernetes kubernetes.md Helm chart, Kind demo, StatefulSet layout

Platform support: Linux (amd64, arm64) and macOS (amd64, arm64) — both natively and in containers. ObjectIO is POSIX-only; there is no native Windows build.

docs.title: Deeper references
docs.text:
• topologies.md — single-node vs rack-aware vs multi-DC; how many disks, nodes, and meta replicas you need for a given EC profile.
  • deployment-options.md — the detailed version: worked scenarios (1, 3, 6+ nodes), EC vs replication, configuration examples, capacity planning.
  • configuration.md — authoritative flag / env / TOML reference for every binary.

docs.title: Minimum requirements
docs.text: Component Minimum Recommended CPU 2 cores 8+ cores per OSD host RAM 4 GB 16+ GB (OSD), 8 GB (meta), 4 GB (gateway) Disk 1 × any block device or file 4+ raw disks per OSD, ≥ 1 TiB each Network 1 Gbps 10+ Gbps between OSDs Linux kernel 4.19+ 5.15+ (io_uring) macOS 12+ — (AIO dev only) Docker 24+ Buildx enabled for multi-arch Kubernetes 1.26+ With a WaitForFirstConsumer StorageClass

docs.title: Cluster sizing at a glance
docs.text:
EC profile Min OSDs Recommended OSDs Meta replicas Survives 4+2 6 7 (+1 spare) 3 2 disk / node failures 8+4 12 14 3 or 5 4 failures 10+4 LRC 14 15 5 4 failures, single-chunk repair replication=3 3 5 3 2 failures (3× overhead)

Meta is a Raft cluster: use 1 pod for dev, 3 for prod, 5 for larger / geo-distributed clusters. Always odd.

docs.title: Default ports (cluster convention)
docs.text:
Port Service Reachable from 9000 Gateway — S3, Iceberg REST, Delta Sharing, /_console/, /_admin/ clients 9100 Meta gRPC + Raft RPC internal 9101 Meta Prometheus /metrics monitoring 9102 Meta admin HTTP (Raft bootstrap / membership) operators 9200 OSD gRPC internal 9201 OSD Prometheus /metrics monitoring 9300 Block gateway gRPC internal 10809 Block gateway NBD target iSCSI / NBD initiators

See configuration.md for the code defaults (which differ for meta and OSD) and how to override them.

docs.title: Security checklist (production)
docs.text:
• [ ] TLS terminated in front of the gateway (ingress / LB / reverse-proxy).
  • [ ] Authentication enabled (--no-auth not set).
  • [ ] OIDC configured for the console + Iceberg JWTs, if applicable.
  • [ ] SSE master key present (gateway.sse.enabled: true in Helm).
  • [ ] Firewall / NetworkPolicy restricting 9100/9101/9200 to the internal network only.
  • [ ] Non-root objectio service user with CAP_SYS_RAWIO (not full root) on OSD nodes.
  • [ ] --trusted-proxies set to the ingress / load balancer network if TLS ends there and policies use aws:SecureTransport or aws:SourceIp.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
1. Pick a deployment path above.
  2. Once running, see the Operations tree for monitoring, metrics, and failure recovery.
  3. And Administration for the admin API surface — users, buckets, warehouses, policies.

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
ObjectIO binaries are configured via CLI flags, a small set of environment variables, and an optional TOML file. Flags win over env vars, env vars win over the TOML file, the TOML file wins over built-in defaults.

This page documents the flag surface for each binary against the current main. It is authoritative over the compose files in deploy/ — some of those files set env vars (OBJECTIO_BIND, OBJECTIO_NODE_ID, etc.) that the binaries do not actually read. Only the env vars listed below are honoured.

docs.title: Ports — cluster conventions vs code defaults
docs.text:
There are two port conventions in the repo. Most deployments follow the cluster convention (used by the Helm chart and the compose files). The CLI flags' code defaults are different:

Role Cluster port Code default Protocol gateway S3 9000 9000 HTTP meta gRPC 9100 9001 gRPC meta metrics 9101 9101 HTTP meta admin (Raft bootstrap / membership) 9102 9102 HTTP OSD gRPC 9200 9002 (example config) gRPC OSD metrics 9201 9201 HTTP block-gateway gRPC 9300 9300 gRPC block-gateway NBD 10809 10809 TCP (NBD)

The chart / compose values are what you should document to end users. The code defaults only matter if you run the binaries standalone with no --listen override.

docs.title: objectio-gateway
docs.text: S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing / admin / console.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
objectio-gateway \
  --listen 0.0.0.0:9000 \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1:9100,http://meta2:9100,http://meta3:9100 \
  --ec-k 4 --ec-m 2 \
  --region us-east-1
Flag Default Purpose -c, --config <path> /etc/objectio/gateway.toml TOML config file -l, --listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:9000 Data plane listen — S3 + Iceberg + Delta Sharing. In legacy mode also serves /_admin/* and /_console/*. --admin-listen <addr> empty Optional dedicated listener for /_admin/* + /metrics. Set this and admin moves off --listen entirely (see Listener split). --ops-console-listen <addr> empty Optional dedicated listener for the ops console SPA + /_admin/* (system-admin surface). --tenant-console-listen <addr> empty Optional dedicated listener for the tenant console SPA + /_admin/* (end-user surface). --meta-endpoint <urls> http://localhost:9001 Meta nodes: one address, or every meta node's, comma-separated. Any node serves any call (a follower forwards it to the Raft leader), and one that stops answering is skipped. See Meta high availability. --osd-endpoint <url> http://localhost:9002 Initial OSD peer --ec-k <n> 4 EC data shards --ec-m <n> 2 EC parity shards --protection <kind> ec ec, lrc, or replication --lrc-local-parity <n> 0 LRC local parity count (with --protection=lrc) --lrc-global-parity <n> 0 LRC global parity count --replicas <n> 3 Replica count (with --protection=replication) --no-auth off Disable SigV4 — dev only --endpoint-name <name> empty Name of the --listen endpoint, seen by policies as aws:SourceVpce (see Public Access). Env OBJECTIO_ENDPOINT_NAME. --data-listen <addr>=<name> — A further data-plane listener (S3, Iceberg, Delta Sharing; no admin, no console) with its own endpoint name. Repeatable. --audit-log <path> unset Append every request's audit event as JSON lines to this file (- for stdout). Env OBJECTIO_AUDIT_LOG. --trusted-proxies <cidrs> empty Proxies whose X-Forwarded-For / X-Forwarded-Proto are believed for aws:SourceIp / aws:SecureTransport. Env OBJECTIO_TRUSTED_PROXIES. Set it when TLS ends at an ingress. --region <name> us-east-1 SigV4 verification region --external-endpoint <url> empty Public URL (Iceberg vended creds, Delta Sharing presign, OIDC callback) --master-key-env <name> OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY Env var name holding the base64 SSE master key --kms-backend <kind> local local or vault --oidc-issuer-url <url> unset Enables OIDC login for console + Iceberg JWTs --oidc-client-id <id> unset OIDC client ID --oidc-client-secret <val> unset OIDC client secret --oidc-audience <val> client id JWT aud expected value --oidc-groups-claim <name> groups Claim mapping to group/role set --oidc-role-claim <name> role Claim mapping to single role --oidc-scopes <scopes> openid profile email Space-separated scope list --oidc-admin-roles <roles> empty Comma-separated list of admin-granting roles --delta-access-key-id <ak> empty Presign AK for Delta Sharing recipient URLs --delta-secret-key <sk> empty Presign SK for Delta Sharing recipient URLs --host-provider <kind> noop noop, k8s, linux-ssh, appliance — powers /_admin/osds/*/reboot --host-provider-namespace <ns> default Namespace for the k8s provider (from $POD_NAMESPACE) --host-provider-osd-sts <name> objectio-osd OSD StatefulSet name for the k8s provider --topology-region <val> empty Gateway's own topology — drives locality-aware reads --topology-zone <val> empty --topology-datacenter <val> empty --topology-rack <val> empty --topology-host <val> empty --log-level <lvl> info trace, debug, info, warn, error

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
The clap parser reads these directly — no wrapper needed:

Env Flag OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_REGION --topology-region OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_ZONE --topology-zone OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_DATACENTER --topology-datacenter OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_RACK --topology-rack OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_HOST --topology-host OBJECTIO_HOST_PROVIDER --host-provider OBJECTIO_HOST_PROVIDER_OSD_STS --host-provider-osd-sts POD_NAMESPACE --host-provider-namespace

Read separately from the flag surface:

Env Purpose OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY 32-byte base64 SSE-S3 master key OBJECTIO_CONSOLE_DIR Path to the legacy single-bundle /_console/ SPA (default /usr/share/objectio/console). In split mode used only as the base for the per-bundle defaults below. OBJECTIO_OPS_CONSOLE_DIR Path to the ops SPA bundle. Default: $OBJECTIO_CONSOLE_DIR/ops. Served on --ops-console-listen. OBJECTIO_TENANT_CONSOLE_DIR Path to the tenant SPA bundle. Default: $OBJECTIO_CONSOLE_DIR/tenant. Served on --tenant-console-listen. RUST_LOG Override --log-level; tracing directive syntax

docs.title: Listener split
docs.text:
By default the gateway is a single-port deployment: --listen carries S3, Iceberg, Delta Sharing, /_admin/*, /metrics, and /_console/* all on the same socket. This matches MinIO's default and is fine for small clusters.

For larger or regulated deployments you can split the four planes across separate listeners by setting any combination of --admin-listen, --ops-console-listen, --tenant-console-listen. Each binds independently; you can enable one, two, or all three.

Listener Default flag Routes mounted Audience data --listen 0.0.0.0:9000 /, /{bucket}*, /iceberg/v1/*, /api/2.1/unity-catalog/*, /delta-sharing/v1/*, /health Public — SDK / CLI / Spark / Trino admin API --admin-listen 127.0.0.1:9001 /_admin/*, /metrics, /health CLI, third-party integrations (Datadog, billing, OTel) ops console --ops-console-listen 127.0.0.1:9002 /_console/* (ops SPA), /_console/api/*, /_admin/*, /health System operators on a mgmt VLAN tenant console --tenant-console-listen 0.0.0.0:9003 /_console/* (tenant SPA), /_console/api/*, /_admin/*, /health End users — safe to expose publicly

Behavior in split mode:

  • /_admin/* is mounted on the admin API listener AND on each console listener (the browser stays same-origin — no CORS). It is removed from the data listener — /_admin/* requests there fall through the S3 wildcard and return SigV4 errors.
  • /metrics lives on the admin API listener only.
  • /_console/* is removed from the data listener; each console listener serves its own SPA bundle from OBJECTIO_OPS_CONSOLE_DIR / OBJECTIO_TENANT_CONSOLE_DIR.
  • The startup log emits a WARN if --admin-listen or --ops-console-listen is bound to 0.0.0.0 — the intent of the split is to firewall the control plane to a mgmt interface.
  • The same /_admin/* handlers run on every listener that mounts them. Per-tenant scope is enforced server-side (see require_tenant_admin_access), so the tenant console listener is not a privilege-elevation path even though it exposes the same surface as the ops console.

Why two consoles, not one with role-gating: see architecture/console-split.

Example — public S3 on the WAN, control plane on a mgmt VLAN:

objectio-gateway \
  --listen                  0.0.0.0:9000 \
  --admin-listen           10.0.5.10:9001 \
  --ops-console-listen     10.0.5.10:9002 \
  --tenant-console-listen   0.0.0.0:9003 \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1:9100 \
  --region us-east-1

Backward compatibility: omit all three split flags and the gateway behaves exactly like pre-split deployments — single port, everything mounted. Existing Helm values and TOML configs continue to work unchanged.

docs.title: objectio-meta
docs.text: Raft metadata cluster.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
objectio-meta \
  --node-id 1 \
  --listen 0.0.0.0:9100 \
  --peers meta1:9101,meta2:9101,meta3:9101 \
  --data-dir /var/lib/objectio/meta
Flag Default Purpose -c, --config <path> /etc/objectio/meta.toml TOML config file --node-id <n> unset Raft node ID (required for multi-node clusters; auto-assigned for single-voter) -l, --listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:9001 gRPC listen — MetadataService + RaftRpc --peers <list> empty Comma-separated Raft peer list (host:port,...) --osd <list> empty Pre-register OSDs on startup (host:port repeated) --ec-k <n> 4 Default EC data shards --ec-m <n> 2 Default EC parity shards --replication <n> unset Use replication instead of EC (1 = single-voter dev mode) --data-dir <path> /var/lib/objectio/meta Persistent Raft + redb state --admin-user <name> admin Initial admin username (created on first startup) --metrics-port <n> 9101 Prometheus scrape port --admin-port <n> 9102 HTTP admin — Raft bootstrap + membership --raft-advertise <addr> empty Address advertised to Raft peers (defaults to --listen) --log-level <lvl> info

--listen vs --raft-advertise: --listen is what the pod binds to locally; --raft-advertise is what it tells peers to reach it at. In Kubernetes the chart sets advertise to the pod DNS (pod-0.meta-svc.ns.svc.cluster.local).

No --raft-bind flag exists — Raft RPC multiplexes over the same gRPC socket as MetadataService.

docs.title: TOML
docs.text:
# /etc/objectio/meta.toml
[meta]
node_id = 1
listen = "0.0.0.0:9100"
peers = ["meta1:9101", "meta2:9101", "meta3:9101"]
data_dir = "/var/lib/objectio/meta"
ec_k = 4
ec_m = 2

[logging]
level = "info"

docs.title: objectio-osd
docs.text: Object Storage Daemon.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
objectio-osd \
  --listen 0.0.0.0:9200 \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1:9100 \
  --disks /dev/sdb,/dev/sdc,/dev/sdd
Flag Default Purpose -c, --config <path> /etc/objectio/osd.toml TOML config file -l, --listen <addr> none gRPC listen — required; cluster convention is :9200 --advertise-addr <addr> none How peers reach this OSD (falls back to listen) --disks <list> empty Explicit disk paths (comma-separated); disables discovery --disk-filter <glob> empty Discovery glob(s), e.g. /dev/disk/by-id/wwn-*; repeatable --disk-min-size <bytes> 1 GiB Lower bound for discovered disks --init-blank-disks off Allow discovery to format blank disks (off by default) --meta-endpoint <url> none Meta service --data-dir <path> none OSD metadata (WAL, object index) --metrics-port <n> 9201 Prometheus scrape port --log-level <lvl> info

docs.title: TOML
docs.text:
# /etc/objectio/osd.toml
[osd]
listen = "0.0.0.0:9200"
meta_endpoint = "http://meta1:9100"

[osd.failure_domain]
region = "eu-west-1"
datacenter = "dc1"
rack = "rack1"

[storage]
disks = ["/dev/sdb", "/dev/sdc", "/dev/sdd"]
# block_size: leave unset. A new disk's allocation unit, 4096 by default;
# every shard takes whole blocks, so a larger one wastes space on small
# objects.
data_dir = "/var/lib/objectio/osd"

[logging]
level = "info"

Disk discovery vs explicit disks. --disks is the production path — list the devices this OSD owns. --disk-filter is for fleets where device names aren't stable (use by-id paths). Without --init-blank-disks, unformatted disks are skipped rather than claimed, as a guard against accidental data loss.

docs.title: objectio-block-gateway
docs.text:
iSCSI / NBD / NVMe-oF target built on top of ObjectIO objects.

objectio-block-gateway \
  --listen 0.0.0.0:9300 \
  --nbd-listen 0.0.0.0:10809 \
  --advertise-host block.internal \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1:9100 \
  --data-dir /var/lib/objectio/block-gw
Flag Default Purpose --listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:9300 BlockService gRPC listen --nbd-listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:10809 NBD TCP listen --advertise-host <host> empty Hostname used in NBD attachment URLs --meta-endpoint <url> http://localhost:9100 --data-dir <path> ./block-gw-data Redb store + journal --cache-bytes <n> 268435456 Write-cache size (256 MiB) --flush-interval-s <n> 5 Background flush interval --ec-k <n> / --ec-m <n> 4 / 2 EC profile for chunk objects --log-level <lvl> info

docs.title: objectio-aio
docs.text:
Single-process cluster (meta + OSD + gateway). See quickstart.md for the full usage.

Flag Default Purpose --port <n> 9000 Public S3 / Iceberg / Delta / console port --listen-addr <ip> 0.0.0.0 Bind interface --data <dir> tempdir Persistent data root --osds <n> 1 Number of OSDs to spawn in-process --auth off Enable SigV4 on the gateway (admin AK/SK printed at startup) --admin-port <n> 0 (off) Mirror of objectio-gateway --admin-listen — bind admin API + /metrics to its own port. --ops-console-port <n> 0 (off) Mirror of --ops-console-listen — serve the ops SPA on its own port. --tenant-console-port <n> 0 (off) Mirror of --tenant-console-listen — serve the tenant SPA on its own port. --endpoint-name <name> empty Mirror of the gateway's --endpoint-name, for --port. --data-port <port>=<name> — Mirror of --data-listen on --listen-addr. Repeatable. --trusted-proxies <cidrs> empty Mirror of the gateway's --trusted-proxies. --audit-log <path> unset Mirror of the gateway's --audit-log. --log-level <lvl> info Honoured only if RUST_LOG is unset --strict-port off Fail on --port conflict instead of picking ephemeral

Pass any of --admin-port / --ops-console-port / --tenant-console-port to test split-mode flows locally. The aio binary embeds both SPA bundles (ops + tenant) at compile time, so no separate console build is needed. With --strict-port set, all configured ports are checked for conflicts before launch.

Example — local split-mode test:

objectio-aio \
  --port 9000 \
  --admin-port 9001 \
  --ops-console-port 9002 \
  --tenant-console-port 9003 \
  --auth --strict-port \
  --data /tmp/objectio-aio

Admin AK/SK are written to <data>/admin-creds.env on first start (keys AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY).

docs.title: objectio-install
docs.text:
Node bootstrapper. See linux.md for a walkthrough.

objectio-install init \
  --role all \
  --disks /dev/sdb,/dev/sdc,/dev/sdd \
  --ec-profile 4+2 \
  --systemd

objectio-install disk list
objectio-install disk prepare /dev/sdb
objectio-install disk check /dev/sdb

objectio-install join \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1.internal:9100 \
  --disks /dev/sdb,/dev/sdc

objectio-install status

init flags:

Flag Default Purpose --role <list> required all, gateway, meta, osd (comma-separated) --disks <list> empty Disk devices for OSD roles --meta-endpoint <url> http://localhost:9001 Used by gateway + OSD roles --raft-peers <list> empty Meta-role peer list --ec-profile <k+m> 4+2 Common profiles: 2+1, 4+2, 8+4, 1+2 (3× replication) --no-auth off Bake no-auth into the generated gateway config --config-dir <dir> /etc/objectio Where config files land --systemd off Install + enable systemd units (requires root) --skip-prepare off Don't touch disks — just render config files --block-size-mb <n> 4 On-disk block size at format time

docs.title: Configuration precedence
docs.text:
For every setting:

  1. CLI flag
  2. Environment variable (if the setting is in the env table above)
  3. TOML file value
  4. Built-in default

So --log-level debug on the command line beats RUST_LOG=info, which beats [logging] level = "warn" in the TOML file.

The meta raft-bootstrap Job and the Helm chart pass settings exclusively through CLI flags in the container command: — if you find yourself reaching for env vars in a compose file, check the list above first; many of the env vars that appear in deploy/local-cluster/docker-compose.yml are not actually read by the binaries.

docs.title: ObjectIO Deployment Options
docs.text: This guide covers deployment configurations based on your hardware topology, in detail; topologies.md is the overview.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Nodes Disks/Node Recommended Config Efficiency Survives 1 12 EC 4+2 (disk-level) 66% 2 disk failures 3 12 EC 6+3 (node-level) 66% 1 node failure 3 12 Replication 3-way 33% 2 node failures 6+ 6+ LRC 6+2+2 (rack-level) 60% 1 rack + 1 disk 10+ 10+ LRC 10+2+2 (rack-level) 71% 1 rack + 1 disk

docs.title: Failure Domain Hierarchy
docs.text:
Region (geo-redundancy)
└── Datacenter (power/network)
    └── Rack (ToR switch, PDU)
        └── Node (server)
            └── Disk (SSD/HDD)

CRUSH spreads shards across the highest available failure domain to maximize fault tolerance.

docs.title: Topology Configuration
docs.text:
Each OSD reports its failure domain on registration. Configure this in /etc/objectio/osd.toml:

[osd]
node_name = "osd-node1"
listen = "0.0.0.0:9002"
meta_endpoint = "http://meta.objectio.local:9001"
weight = 1.0

# Failure domain - where this OSD sits in the hierarchy
[osd.failure_domain]
region = "us-east"        # Geographic region
datacenter = "dc1"        # Data center or AZ
rack = "rack-01"          # Physical rack

[storage]
disks = ["/mnt/nvme0", "/mnt/nvme1", ...]

How CRUSH uses this:

  1. OSDs register with their failure domain
  2. Metadata service builds a topology tree
  3. When placing shards, CRUSH ensures each shard lands in a different failure domain at the configured level
  4. If failure_domain = "rack", no two shards of the same object share a rack

See examples/config/ for complete configuration examples.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Single Node (12 Disks)
docs.text:
Hardware: 1 server with 12 disks

Failure Domain: Disk-level only (can't survive node failure)

docs.title: Option 1B: EC 8+4 (Maximum Fault Tolerance)
docs.text:
Configuration:
  ec_k: 8          # Data shards
  ec_m: 4          # Parity shards
  ec_type: MDS
  failure_domain: disk
Metric Value Storage efficiency 66% (8/12) Fault tolerance 4 disk failures Min disks 12 Read performance Parallel from 8 disks Repair cost Read 8 shards, write 1

docs.title: Option 1C: Replication 3-way (Simple, Lower Efficiency)
docs.text:
Configuration:
  ec_k: 1          # Single data copy
  ec_m: 2          # Two additional replicas
  ec_type: MDS     # (Replication is k=1 EC)
  failure_domain: disk
Metric Value Storage efficiency 33% (1/3) Fault tolerance 2 disk failures Min disks 3 Read performance Single disk (can load-balance) Repair cost Read 1, write 1

When to use replication: - Small objects (< 1MB) where EC overhead dominates - Random read workloads where single-disk latency matters - Simplest operational model

docs.title: Scenario 2: Three Nodes (12 Disks Each)
docs.text:
Hardware: 3 servers, each with 12 disks (36 total disks)

Failure Domain Options: - Node-level: Survive 1 complete node failure - Disk-level: Survive multiple disk failures across nodes

docs.title: Option 2A: EC 6+3 Node-Level (Recommended)
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│   Node 0 (12 disks)    │   Node 1 (12 disks)    │   Node 2 (12 disks)  │
│  ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐    │  ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐    │  ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐  │
│  │ D0 ││ D1 ││ D2 │    │  │ D3 ││ D4 ││ D5 │    │  │ P0 ││ P1 ││ P2 │  │
│  └────┘└────┘└────┘    │  └────┘└────┘└────┘    │  └────┘└────┘└────┘  │
│                        │                        │                      │
│  Each node gets 3      │  Each node gets 3      │  Each node gets 3    │
│  shards per object     │  shards per object     │  shards per object   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Configuration:
  ec_k: 6          # Data shards
  ec_m: 3          # Parity shards
  ec_type: MDS
  failure_domain: node
Metric Value Storage efficiency 66% (6/9) Fault tolerance 1 node OR 3 disks Min nodes 3 Shards per node 3 Read performance Parallel from 2+ nodes Repair cost Read 6 shards (cross-node)

Math: With 3 nodes and k=6, m=3: - 9 shards ÷ 3 nodes = 3 shards per node - Node failure loses 3 shards = exactly m - Can reconstruct from remaining 6 shards ✓

docs.title: Option 2C: Replication 3-way (Maximum Availability)
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│   Node 0               │   Node 1               │   Node 2              │
│  ┌────────────────┐    │  ┌────────────────┐    │  ┌────────────────┐   │
│  │   Full Copy    │    │  │   Full Copy    │    │  │   Full Copy    │   │
│  │   (Primary)    │    │  │   (Replica 1)  │    │  │   (Replica 2)  │   │
│  └────────────────┘    │  └────────────────┘    │  └────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Configuration:
  ec_k: 1
  ec_m: 2
  ec_type: MDS
  failure_domain: node
Metric Value Storage efficiency 33% (1/3) Fault tolerance 2 node failures Read performance Any single node (load-balance) Write performance Must write to all 3 nodes

Use replication when: - Data durability is paramount (financial, medical) - Random read latency is critical - Simple operational model preferred over efficiency

docs.title: Scenario 3: Six+ Nodes (Multi-Rack with LRC)
docs.text:
Hardware: 6+ servers across multiple racks

Failure Domain: Rack-level (survive ToR switch or PDU failure)

docs.title: Option 3A: LRC 6+2+2 (Recommended for 6+ Nodes)
docs.text:
LRC (Locally Repairable Codes) adds local parity within groups for faster single-failure repair.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                              LRC 6+2+2                                   │
│                                                                         │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │        Local Group 0         │  │        Local Group 1         │     │
│  │  ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐   │  │  ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐   │     │
│  │  │ D0 ││ D1 ││ D2 ││ LP0│   │  │  │ D3 ││ D4 ││ D5 ││ LP1│   │     │
│  │  │Rk0 ││Rk0 ││Rk0 ││Rk0 │   │  │  │Rk1 ││Rk1 ││Rk1 ││Rk1 │   │     │
│  │  └────┘└────┘└────┘└────┘   │  │  └────┘└────┘└────┘└────┘   │     │
│  └──────────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                         │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│  │       Global Parity          │                                       │
│  │  ┌────┐┌────┐               │                                       │
│  │  │GP0 ││GP1 │               │  GP = Reed-Solomon over all data      │
│  │  │Rk2 ││Rk2 │               │                                       │
│  │  └────┘└────┘               │                                       │
│  └──────────────────────────────┘                                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Configuration:
  ec_k: 6              # Data shards
  ec_type: LRC
  ec_local_parity: 2   # One per local group
  ec_global_parity: 2  # Reed-Solomon over all data
  local_group_size: 3  # Data shards per local group
  failure_domain: rack
Metric Value Storage efficiency 60% (6/10) Total shards 10 (6 data + 2 LP + 2 GP) Fault tolerance 1 rack + 1 disk, OR 4 disks Local repair Read 3 shards (within rack) Global repair Read 6 shards (cross-rack)

LRC Repair Scenarios:

Failure Type Repair Method Network Cost 1 data disk XOR with local parity Read 3 (local) 1 local parity disk XOR with data shards Read 3 (local) 2 disks same group Reed-Solomon global Read 6 (cross-rack) 1 disk + 1 LP (diff) Local + Local Read 6 (2×3 local) Full rack failure Reed-Solomon global Read 6 (cross-rack)

docs.title: Option 3B: LRC 10+2+2 (Higher Efficiency)
docs.text:
Configuration:
  ec_k: 10             # Data shards
  ec_type: LRC
  ec_local_parity: 2   # One per local group
  ec_global_parity: 2
  local_group_size: 5  # 5 data shards per group
  failure_domain: rack
Metric Value Storage efficiency 71% (10/14) Total shards 14 (10 data + 2 LP + 2 GP) Min racks 4 (5+1 per local group + GP) Local repair Read 5 shards (within rack)

docs.title: Single Node (12 disks) - EC 4+2
docs.text:
# /etc/objectio/osd.toml
[osd]
node_name = "osd-single"
listen = "0.0.0.0:9002"
meta_endpoint = "http://localhost:9001"

# Single node: all OSDs share the same failure domain
# CRUSH spreads shards across different DISKS
[osd.failure_domain]
region = "default"
datacenter = "dc1"
rack = "rack1"

[storage]
data_dir = "/var/lib/objectio/osd"
disks = [
  "/mnt/nvme0", "/mnt/nvme1", "/mnt/nvme2", "/mnt/nvme3",
  "/mnt/nvme4", "/mnt/nvme5", "/mnt/nvme6", "/mnt/nvme7",
  "/mnt/nvme8", "/mnt/nvme9", "/mnt/nvme10", "/mnt/nvme11"
]

Gateway config:

# /etc/objectio/gateway.toml - EC 4+2 for single node
ec_k = 4
ec_m = 2

docs.title: Three Nodes - EC 6+3
docs.text:
Each node needs a different rack in its failure domain:

# Node 1: /etc/objectio/osd.toml
[osd]
node_name = "osd-node1"
listen = "0.0.0.0:9002"
meta_endpoint = "http://meta.objectio.local:9001"

[osd.failure_domain]
region = "us-east"
datacenter = "dc1"
rack = "rack-01"        # <-- Different rack per node!

[storage]
disks = ["/mnt/nvme0", "/mnt/nvme1", ..., "/mnt/nvme11"]

# Node 2: /etc/objectio/osd.toml
[osd.failure_domain]
region = "us-east"
datacenter = "dc1"
rack = "rack-02"        # <-- Different rack

# Node 3: /etc/objectio/osd.toml
[osd.failure_domain]
region = "us-east"
datacenter = "dc1"
rack = "rack-03"        # <-- Different rack

Gateway config:

# /etc/objectio/gateway.toml - EC 6+3 for three nodes
ec_k = 6
ec_m = 3

docs.title: Six+ Nodes - LRC 6+2+2
docs.text:
# /etc/objectio/gateway.toml
ec_k = 6
ec_local_parity = 2
ec_global_parity = 2
local_group_size = 3

See examples/config/ for complete, ready-to-use configuration files.

docs.title: Usable Capacity Formula
docs.text:
Usable = Raw × (k / (k + m))        # For MDS
Usable = Raw × (k / (k + l + g))    # For LRC

docs.title: Example: 3 Nodes × 12 Disks × 10TB
docs.text: Config Raw Capacity Efficiency Usable Capacity Replication 3 360 TB 33% 120 TB EC 4+2 360 TB 66% 240 TB EC 6+3 360 TB 66% 240 TB LRC 6+2+2 360 TB 60% 216 TB

docs.title: IOPS Considerations
docs.text: Config Read IOPS (per object) Write IOPS (per object) Replication 3 1 disk (can load-balance) 3 disks (all replicas) EC 4+2 4 disks (parallel) 6 disks (parallel) EC 6+3 6 disks (parallel) 9 disks (parallel) LRC 6+2+2 6 disks (parallel) 10 disks (parallel)

docs.title: Starting Small, Growing Large
docs.text:
Phase 1: Single node, 6 disks
  └── EC 4+2 (disk-level)
         │
         ▼
Phase 2: 3 nodes, 12 disks each
  └── EC 6+3 (node-level)
         │
         ▼
Phase 3: 6+ nodes across racks
  └── LRC 6+2+2 (rack-level)

Data migration: ObjectIO supports online rebalancing when topology changes. Adding nodes triggers gradual data movement via background repair.

docs.title: Summary Recommendations
docs.text: Deployment Size Recommended Config Why Dev/Test Single node, EC 4+2 Simple, efficient, survives disk failures Small Prod 3 nodes, EC 6+3 Survives node failure, good efficiency Medium Prod 6 nodes, LRC 6+2+2 Fast local repair, rack-level tolerance Large Prod 10+ nodes, LRC 10+2+2 Best efficiency (71%), scalable Critical 3-way replication Maximum durability, simple operations

docs.text:
