docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
ObjectIO ships a single multi-stage Dockerfile that produces six targets. You pick one image per role (three for a minimal split-role cluster, six if you want the block gateway too), or the all-in-one image for quick-test / appliance setups.

  • Fastest demo: objectio-aio container
  • Real local cluster: make cluster-up (3 meta + 6 OSD + 1 gateway, 4+2 EC)
  • Production-shaped raw disks: deploy/prod/
  • Kubernetes: see kubernetes.md

docs.title: Image targets
docs.text:
Target Binary Ports Role gateway objectio-gateway 9000 S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing / /_console/ meta objectio-meta 9100 (gRPC), 9101 (Raft), 9102 (admin) Raft metadata osd objectio-osd 9200 (gRPC), 9201 (metrics) Object storage daemon cli obioctl — Admin CLI block-gateway objectio-block-gateway 9300 (gRPC), 10809 (NBD) iSCSI / NBD / NVMe-oF target all all of the above 9000 + internal One image, any binary (AIO image)

Port numbers are the cluster convention used by deploy/ and the Helm chart. The CLI defaults inside each binary are different (gateway/meta/osd default to 9000/9001/9002). See configuration.md for the split.

One multi-arch image is published on GHCR, and it carries every service:

  • ghcr.io/object-io/objectio:latest (the all target)

Each container overrides the entrypoint to pick a service — that is what the helm chart does. The per-service Dockerfile targets (gateway, meta, osd, cli, block-gateway) are not published; build them locally if you want them:

docker build --target gateway -t objectio-gateway .

linux/amd64 uses ISA-L for hardware-accelerated erasure coding; linux/arm64 uses pure-Rust SIMD. Mixing arches in a cluster is supported.

docs.title: All-in-one (AIO) image
docs.text:
The all target packages every binary plus the console SPA. You choose the entrypoint at docker run time.

# Run AIO — single-process cluster, everything on port 9000
docker run --rm -p 9000:9000 \
  -v objectio-data:/var/lib/objectio \
  ghcr.io/object-io/objectio:latest \
  objectio-aio --data /var/lib/objectio

# Same image, run the admin CLI against an existing cluster
docker run --rm --network host \
  ghcr.io/object-io/objectio:latest \
  -e OBJECTIO_ACCESS_KEY -e OBJECTIO_SECRET_KEY \
  obioctl --endpoint http://localhost:9000 user list

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text: Use AIO image Use split images Laptop dev, CI, demos, smoke tests Production Single-process topology Separate pods / nodes per role One binary, any subcommand Minimal attack surface per container

docs.title: Local cluster (make cluster-up)
docs.text:
deploy/local-cluster/docker-compose.yml stands up the shape people actually run: 3 meta replicas (real Raft), 6 OSDs (for 4+2 EC), 1 gateway, 1 block-gateway, all on one Docker host.

git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio

make cluster-up          # builds images, starts the stack
make cluster-status      # docker compose ps
make cluster-logs        # tail every service
make cluster-cli ARGS="user list"    # run obioctl in the cluster network
make cluster-down        # stop, keep volumes
make cluster-clean       # stop + wipe volumes

Direct docker compose also works:

docker compose -f deploy/local-cluster/docker-compose.yml up -d
docker compose -f deploy/local-cluster/docker-compose.yml logs -f gateway

docs.title: Ports exposed on the host
docs.text:
Host port Container Purpose 9000 gateway:9000 S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing / /_console/ 9100 meta1:9100 Meta gRPC (leader usually talks here) 9102 / 9103 meta2:9100 / meta3:9100 Meta gRPC (followers) 9200 + 9202–9206 osd1..osd6:9200 OSD gRPC 9300 block-gateway:9300 Block gRPC 10809 block-gateway:10809 NBD target

Nothing else is exposed — meta's Raft port (9101) and per-OSD metrics ports are only reachable inside the objectio-net bridge.

docs.title: Monitoring side-car
docs.text:
An optional companion compose file layers on Prometheus + Grafana:

docker compose \
  -f deploy/local-cluster/docker-compose.yml \
  -f deploy/local-cluster/docker-compose.monitoring.yml \
  up -d
# Grafana: http://localhost:3000  (admin / objectio)

docs.title: Production compose (raw disks)
docs.text:
deploy/prod/docker-compose.yml is a reference for running ObjectIO on a single host with real block devices rather than volumes. Use it as a starting point for appliance builds or when Kubernetes is overkill.

Key differences from the local-cluster compose:

  • OSDs run privileged: true with SYS_RAWIO + SYS_ADMIN. The storage engine needs O_DIRECT and ioctl BLKGETSIZE64 against raw disks, which the default Docker cap set denies.
  • Disks are passed as devices:, not volumes:.
  • DISK_MODE=raw|folder toggles between real disks and sparse file "disks" for testing.
# Edit deploy/prod/docker-compose.yml to list your actual devices
# (/dev/nvme0n1, /dev/sdb, etc.) under each osdN's `devices:` block.

DISK_MODE=raw docker compose -f deploy/prod/docker-compose.yml up -d

deploy/single-node-7disk/ is a worked example: a 7-disk single box, one disk per OSD container, including setup-disks.sh for mkfs/fstab prep and deploy.sh for remote SSH deployment.

docs.title: Building images locally
docs.text:
# Single-arch, native platform
make docker                 # all targets
make docker-gateway         # just the gateway
make docker-all             # the AIO image

# Multi-arch (requires docker buildx, pushes to registry)
DOCKER_REGISTRY=ghcr.io/myorg/ DOCKER_TAG=v1.0.0 \
  make docker-multiarch

# Multi-arch local-only (current platform, loads into Docker)
make docker-multiarch-local

Build args exposed by the Dockerfile:

Arg Default Notes RUST_VERSION 1.93 Rust compiler pinned in the builder-base stage FEATURES auto isal on x86_64, empty on arm64. Override to force either. TARGETPLATFORM / TARGETARCH from buildx Set automatically by docker buildx

Example — build a pure-Rust amd64 image (useful for platforms that lack the ISA-L nasm prereq):

docker build --target all --build-arg FEATURES="" -t objectio:no-isal .

docs.title: Environment variables (containerised services)
docs.text:
Most configuration goes via CLI flags in the container command: block — see the compose files in deploy/ for worked examples. A small set of settings is additionally reachable via env vars:

Env var Service Purpose OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_REGION gateway Sets --topology-region OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_ZONE gateway Sets --topology-zone OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_DATACENTER gateway Sets --topology-datacenter OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_RACK gateway Sets --topology-rack OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_HOST gateway Sets --topology-host OBJECTIO_HOST_PROVIDER gateway Sets --host-provider (noop | k8s) OBJECTIO_HOST_PROVIDER_OSD_STS gateway OSD StatefulSet name (k8s provider only) POD_NAMESPACE gateway Namespace for host-provider RBAC (k8s only) OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY gateway SSE-S3 master key (base64 32-byte) OBJECTIO_CONSOLE_DIR gateway Override the /_console/ static-asset dir RUST_LOG all Overrides --log-level; same syntax as tracing

For everything else — listen address, meta endpoint, EC profile, data dir — pass flags in command:. See configuration.md for the full CLI surface.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
Built into every runtime image:

# gateway
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:9000/health || exit 1
# meta, osd, block-gateway
HEALTHCHECK CMD /usr/local/bin/healthcheck.sh      # stub — always exits 0

The gateway health check is the real one (queries /health which checks meta connectivity). Meta / OSD currently rely on their supervisor (compose restart policy, or K8s liveness probes in the Helm chart) to restart on crash.

docs.title: "operation not permitted" on an OSD
docs.text:
OSDs need CAP_SYS_RAWIO to open raw block devices with O_DIRECT. In docker-compose.yml:

services:
  osd1:
    privileged: true   # easiest — or scope down to:
    cap_add: [SYS_RAWIO, SYS_ADMIN]
    devices: [/dev/sdb:/dev/sdb]

docs.title: Gateway can't reach meta
docs.text:
Gateways and OSDs take every meta node's address in one comma-separated --meta-endpoint (for example http://meta1:9100,http://meta2:9100,http://meta3:9100); any one that answers serves them. Confirm DNS resolves inside the objectio-net bridge:

docker compose -f deploy/local-cluster/docker-compose.yml exec gateway \
  getent hosts meta1

docs.title: "port already in use" on cluster-up
docs.text: Something else is bound to 9000 / 9100 / 9200–9206 / 9300 / 10809. Either stop the conflicting service or change host port mappings in the compose file.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
ObjectIO ships a first-class Helm chart at deploy/helm/objectio/ in the source repo. It wraps every component — gateway (Deployment), meta (StatefulSet, 1 or 3+ pods with Raft bootstrap Job), OSD (StatefulSet with per-pod PVCs), optional block-gateway, optional Prometheus + Grafana — into one release.

This page is the operator-side walkthrough. For a kubectl demo on a laptop, use the Kind path at the bottom.

Audience Start here Trying it on a laptop Kind walkthrough Production install Install the chart Tuning an existing release values.yaml reference

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Kubernetes 1.26+ (kubeVersion in Chart.yaml)
  • Helm 3.11+
  • A StorageClass that supports ReadWriteOnce and, ideally, WaitForFirstConsumer binding (so OSD pods schedule on nodes with real local disks). Cloud defaults (EBS gp3, PD-SSD, Premium-LRS) work; local-path / Rancher local provisioner is fine for testing only.
  • For ingress: an ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik) or a Gateway API implementation.
  • If you want the k8s-native host-lifecycle provider (gateway admin API Add Host / Reboot OSD), the chart creates its own ServiceAccount + Role. Your cluster just needs RBAC enabled.

No external dependencies (etcd, ZooKeeper, Redis) — meta is a self-contained Raft cluster.

docs.title: Installing the chart
docs.text:
The chart isn't in a public Helm repo yet. Install from a checkout:

git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio

helm install objectio ./deploy/helm/objectio \
  --namespace objectio --create-namespace \
  --values my-values.yaml \
  --wait --timeout 10m

Check it came up:

kubectl -n objectio get pods
# NAME                              READY   STATUS
# objectio-gateway-<hash>           1/1     Running
# objectio-meta-0                   1/1     Running
# objectio-meta-1                   1/1     Running
# objectio-meta-2                   1/1     Running
# objectio-osd-0 … objectio-osd-5   1/1     Running

Expose the gateway however your cluster does it — NodePort, LoadBalancer, or kubectl port-forward:

kubectl -n objectio port-forward svc/objectio-gateway 9000:9000
# then:  aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 ls

The first admin AK/SK is written by the post-install job to a Secret named objectio-admin-creds (keys: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY).

docs.title: values.yaml reference
docs.text: The chart has a wide surface. These are the stanzas you'll actually touch; the full default is in deploy/helm/objectio/values.yaml in the source repo.

docs.title: Scale and durability
docs.text:
ec:
  k: 4            # data shards
  m: 2            # parity shards

meta:
  replicas: 3     # 1 = single-voter (dev); 3+ = real Raft (prod)

osd:
  replicas: 6     # must be >= k + m; set to k+m+spare for repair headroom

Minimum OSD replicas for common EC profiles:

Profile OSDs Spare recommended 4+2 6 7 8+4 12 14 10+4 (LRC) 14 15

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text:
gateway:
  replicas: 2                          # stateless, scale for throughput
  noAuth: false                        # true only for dev
  region: us-east-1
  externalUrl: https://s3.example.com  # used by Iceberg vended creds + Delta Sharing presign
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    className: nginx
    hosts:
      - host: s3.example.com
        paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }]
    tls:
      - hosts: [s3.example.com]
        secretName: s3-tls
  oidc:
    issuerUrl: https://keycloak.example.com/realms/objectio
    clientId: objectio
    clientSecret: ""      # or via existingSecret
    adminRoles: objectio-admin
  sse:
    enabled: true         # generates + mounts OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY on first install
  topology:
    region: eu-west-1
    zone: eu-west-1a
    datacenter: dc1
    rack: ""              # usually auto-derived from node topology labels
  hostProvider:
    enabled: true
    kind: k8s             # lets /_admin/osds/*/reboot actually reboot pods
  # Name the endpoints, for policies that depend on where a request came
  # from (aws:SourceVpce). With external.port set, the ingress targets that
  # port, so pods (the Service on 9000) and the outside (the ingress) arrive
  # on different, named endpoints.
  endpoints:
    internalName: internal
    external:
      port: 9010
      name: external
  # The ingress controller's pod network: its X-Forwarded-For and
  # X-Forwarded-Proto are believed (aws:SourceIp, aws:SecureTransport).
  trustedProxies: "10.244.0.0/16"

New buckets start with public access blocked, and a bucket can be readable without keys from inside the cluster only. See Public Access.

docs.title: OSD — failure domains and persistence
docs.text:
Each OSD pod gets two PVCs: a data PVC (holds the disk.raw backing file, or gets mounted over by a hostPath device) and a small state PVC (WAL + superblock copy). Sizing the data PVC drives cluster capacity.

osd:
  replicas: 6
  failureDomain:
    region: eu-west-1
    datacenter: dc1
    rack: rack1           # override per-node via pod topology labels
  storage:
    diskFile: disk.raw    # blockSize: leave unset (the OSD's 4 KiB)
  persistence:
    data:
      size: 1Ti
      storageClass: gp3
    state:
      size: 5Gi
      storageClass: gp3
  resources:
    requests: { cpu: "1",  memory: 2Gi }
    limits:   { cpu: "4",  memory: 8Gi }

For bare-metal / local-disk OSDs, use a local or topolvm StorageClass with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer so each OSD schedules on a node whose disk it can bind to. Cloud EBS-style classes work out of the box.

docs.title: Meta — Raft
docs.text:
meta:
  replicas: 3                    # 1 or 3+; do not use 2 or other even numbers
  persistence:
    size: 50Gi
    storageClass: gp3
  resources:
    requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: 1Gi }
    limits:   { cpu: "2",    memory: 4Gi }

The chart includes a meta-raft-bootstrap-job that runs once on first install. It waits for all meta-* pods to become ready, then issues the Raft membership seed RPC against meta-0. Re-running helm install on a pre-existing release is idempotent; the Job detects an already-bootstrapped cluster and exits.

docs.title: Block gateway (iSCSI / NBD)
docs.text:
Opt-in; off by default.

blockGateway:
  enabled: true
  replicas: 1
  advertiseHost: block.svc.cluster.local   # hostname initiators will attach to
  cacheBytes: 268435456                    # 256 MiB write cache
  service:
    type: LoadBalancer                     # NBD is TCP — must be reachable
    nbdPort: 10809

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Self-contained Prometheus + Grafana stack. Off by default; turn on for quick demos. For real deployments, point your existing Prometheus at the /metrics endpoints (ServiceMonitor templates are in the chart).

monitoring:
  enabled: true
  grafana:
    adminPassword: "<rotate-me>"
  prometheus:
    retention: 30d
    persistence: { size: 50Gi }

docs.title: Storage class guidance
docs.text:
Disk topology StorageClass Notes Cloud block storage (EBS gp3, PD-SSD) default PVC = 1 disk = 1 OSD Local NVMe via local-static-provisioner local-storage, WaitForFirstConsumer pin OSDs to disk-owning nodes with nodeAffinity Local NVMe via TopoLVM topolvm-provisioner LVM-backed, dynamic Ceph RBD on the same cluster don't You're storage-on-storage; use ObjectIO directly

Avoid putting OSDs on NFS / object-backed volumes — the storage engine's durability contract assumes local-ish block semantics.

docs.title: Scaling an existing release
docs.text:
# Add OSDs (e.g. 6 → 9 for 8+4 EC)
helm upgrade objectio ./deploy/helm/objectio -n objectio \
  --reuse-values \
  --set osd.replicas=9 \
  --set ec.k=8 --set ec.m=4

Meta cluster membership changes (1 → 3, or replacing a meta pod) are coordinated by the chart's meta-raft-bootstrap-job on upgrade. Changes to OSD count trigger a rebalance; see operations/failure-recovery.md for progress + throttling knobs.

docs.title: Losing a meta pod
docs.text: With three metas, any one pod can go (killed, evicted, rescheduled, or rolled by kubectl rollout restart) without losing anything the gateway acknowledged. If it was the leader, the other two elect one in about 5 seconds; writes that arrive meanwhile get 503 ServiceUnavailable, which S3 clients retry, and resume on their own. The pod comes back on its PVC and catches up. Losing two of three at once stops writes until one returns: keep the PodDisruptionBudget (meta.podDisruptionBudget) on.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
helm uninstall objectio -n objectio
# PVCs are NOT deleted by default — protects against accidental data loss:
kubectl -n objectio delete pvc -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=objectio
kubectl delete namespace objectio

docs.title: Kind (local Kubernetes) walkthrough
docs.text:
deploy/kind/setup.sh is a one-shot script that stands up a 3-node Kind cluster (1 control-plane + 2 workers), builds every image, loads them into the cluster, installs the chart with a Kind-tuned values.yaml, port-forwards the gateway to localhost:9000, and runs a smoke test covering S3 + Iceberg + Delta Sharing.

# Prereqs: docker, kind, kubectl, helm
git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio

make kind-up                                 # build + deploy from source
# OR
make kind-up-registry                        # pull from ghcr.io/object-io (no local build)

If something already listens on port 9000, forward the gateway elsewhere: PF_PORT=19000 make kind-up.

To check meta HA on it, with S3 traffic running from a pod: kill the meta leader's pod, then a follower's, then roll the StatefulSet; every acknowledged write must read back.

deploy/kind/meta-ha-test.sh

When it finishes, the script prints:

Endpoints (via kubectl port-forward):
  S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing  http://localhost:9000
  Grafana                       http://localhost:3000   (admin / objectio)

EC scheme: 4+2  |  Meta: 3 nodes  |  OSDs: 6 nodes

docs.title: Teardown and re-deploy
docs.text:
make kind-down             # delete the whole Kind cluster
make kind-load             # rebuild images + reload into a running cluster
kubectl -n objectio rollout restart statefulset/objectio-osd  # pick up new images

docs.title: Why Kind defaults may not match prod
docs.text:
• EC 4+2 on a 3-node Kind means multiple OSDs per node — failure domains are enforced at disk (PVC) level, not host.
  • standard StorageClass is Kind's local-path provisioner. Fine for tests, unusable for real durability.
  • Gateway has noAuth: true — SigV4 is disabled. Never promote this values file to a real cluster.

For a production-realistic K8s install, use the main deploy/helm/objectio/values.yaml with your own overrides as shown above.

docs.title: OSD pods stuck Pending
docs.text: Usually a PVC that can't bind. kubectl -n objectio describe pvc — most common causes: no default StorageClass, or WaitForFirstConsumer + nodeAffinity can't find a matching node.

docs.title: meta-0 crash-loops with "node not in cluster"
docs.text:
The raft-bootstrap Job didn't complete. Check:

kubectl -n objectio logs job/objectio-meta-raft-bootstrap
kubectl -n objectio get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/component=meta -o wide

All three meta pods must be Ready before the Job issues the seed RPC. If the Job failed (e.g. network policy blocking pod → pod traffic), re-run it:

kubectl -n objectio delete job objectio-meta-raft-bootstrap
helm upgrade objectio ./deploy/helm/objectio -n objectio --reuse-values

docs.title: kubectl port-forward drops connections
docs.text: Use a Service of type: LoadBalancer (on clouds) or a proper ingress in production. port-forward is for dev only.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Linux is the primary production target. Both amd64 and arm64 are first-class — amd64 gets hardware-accelerated erasure coding via ISA-L, arm64 uses a pure-Rust SIMD implementation. Wire format is identical; you can mix architectures in a cluster.

This page covers the three installation paths, in increasing order of commitment:

  1. Release binaries — drop-in objectio-* binaries
  2. objectio-install — automated node bootstrap with systemd units
  3. From source — Rust toolchain, for contributors

If you just want a quick local endpoint, use objectio-aio — one binary, no daemons. The rest of this page is about real multi-process / multi-node deployments.

docs.title: System requirements
docs.text:
Component Minimum Recommended Kernel 4.19+ 5.15+ (for io_uring) CPU 2 cores 8+ cores RAM 4 GB 16+ GB (OSD), 8 GB (meta), 4 GB (gateway) Disks (OSD) 1 × any block device 4+ dedicated raw disks per OSD node Network 1 Gbps 10+ Gbps (especially between OSDs)

Filesystem: OSDs prefer raw block devices (/dev/sdb, /dev/nvme0n1). File-backed disks (/mnt/.../disk.raw) work but skip the O_DIRECT fast path and lose some durability guarantees. Disks are formatted with ObjectIO's own on-disk layout (superblock + WAL + blocks), not ext4/xfs — mkfs-ing first is not required and is not recommended for production OSDs.

Kernel features used:

  • O_DIRECT on raw block devices (required for OSD disks)
  • ioctl BLKGETSIZE64 for disk sizing
  • io_uring when available (5.15+); falls back to threaded I/O

Supported distributions: any glibc 2.31+ (Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+, RHEL 9+, Amazon Linux 2023, Rocky/Alma 9+). For older glibc, build from source.

docs.title: 1. Release binaries
docs.text:
Released binaries are statically linked except for glibc and OpenSSL. Pick the right arch:

ARCH=$(uname -m | sed 's/x86_64/amd64/;s/aarch64/arm64/')
curl -L -o /tmp/objectio.tar.gz \
  https://github.com/object-io/objectio/releases/latest/download/objectio-linux-${ARCH}.tar.gz
sudo tar -xzf /tmp/objectio.tar.gz -C /usr/local/bin \
  objectio-aio objectio-gateway objectio-meta objectio-osd obioctl \
  objectio-install objectio-block-gateway

Verify:

obioctl --version
objectio-aio --help

Runtime packages (all installed automatically as dependencies of the systemd unit on RPM/DEB-based distros, or install manually for the tarball):

# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates libssl3

# RHEL / Rocky / Alma 9+
sudo dnf install -y ca-certificates openssl-libs

docs.title: 2. Bootstrapping a node with objectio-install
docs.text: objectio-install is the one-shot node bootstrapper. It prepares disks, writes config files, and optionally installs and enables systemd units. Use it for fresh metal / VMs.

docs.title: Create the service user
docs.text:
sudo groupadd -r objectio
sudo useradd -r -g objectio -d /var/lib/objectio -s /usr/sbin/nologin objectio
sudo mkdir -p /etc/objectio /var/lib/objectio /var/log/objectio
sudo chown objectio:objectio /var/lib/objectio /var/log/objectio

docs.title: Inspect candidate disks
docs.text:
sudo objectio-install disk list           # only unused disks
sudo objectio-install disk list --all     # everything, including mounted ones

Output shows path, size, model, and whether the disk already contains an ObjectIO superblock. objectio-install disk prepare is destructive — it overwrites the device with a fresh superblock.

sudo objectio-install disk prepare /dev/sdb --block-size-mb 4
sudo objectio-install disk check /dev/sdb   # verify

docs.title: Initialize the node
docs.text:
The init subcommand generates /etc/objectio/{gateway,meta,osd}.toml and (with --systemd) installs /etc/systemd/system/objectio-*.service.

Single-node (all roles on one box, good for edge / appliance):

sudo objectio-install init \
  --role all \
  --disks /dev/sdb,/dev/sdc,/dev/sdd,/dev/sde,/dev/sdf,/dev/sdg \
  --ec-profile 4+2 \
  --systemd
sudo systemctl enable --now objectio-meta objectio-osd objectio-gateway

Meta node (Raft):

sudo objectio-install init \
  --role meta \
  --raft-peers meta1.internal:9101,meta2.internal:9101,meta3.internal:9101 \
  --systemd
sudo systemctl enable --now objectio-meta

OSD node (storage):

sudo objectio-install init \
  --role osd \
  --disks /dev/sdb,/dev/sdc,/dev/sdd,/dev/sde \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1.internal:9100,http://meta2.internal:9100,http://meta3.internal:9100 \
  --systemd
sudo systemctl enable --now objectio-osd

Gateway node (S3 API):

sudo objectio-install init \
  --role gateway \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1.internal:9100,http://meta2.internal:9100,http://meta3.internal:9100 \
  --systemd
sudo systemctl enable --now objectio-gateway

docs.title: Joining an existing cluster
docs.text:
Skip config generation; point at the running meta and attach the local disks:

sudo objectio-install join \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1.internal:9100,http://meta2.internal:9100,http://meta3.internal:9100 \
  --disks /dev/sdb,/dev/sdc

docs.title: What gets written
docs.text:
Path Purpose /etc/objectio/gateway.toml / meta.toml / osd.toml Per-service config /etc/systemd/system/objectio-*.service systemd units (if --systemd) /var/lib/objectio/{meta,osd}/ Persistent state /var/log/objectio/ Log output (journald in parallel)

objectio-install status shows the current config + detected roles.

docs.title: 3. Build from source
docs.text: Needed if you want to track main, run a custom branch, or build for an older glibc.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text:
# Rust (1.93+)
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
rustup toolchain install 1.93

# Build deps
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt-get install -y build-essential nasm autoconf automake libtool \
  libclang-dev pkg-config protobuf-compiler libprotobuf-dev cmake

# RHEL / Rocky / Alma 9+
sudo dnf install -y gcc-c++ make nasm autoconf automake libtool \
  clang-devel pkgconf protobuf-compiler protobuf-devel cmake

NASM is only required on x86_64 — it drives ISA-L's assembly. On ARM64 omit it and drop --features isal.

docs.title: Console (SPA) prerequisites
docs.text:
objectio-aio and the gateway's /_console/ surface embed a pre-built React bundle. If you're only building server binaries and don't need the console, nothing to do. To build the console you need Node 22+:

# Ubuntu — NodeSource 22.x
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt-get install -y nodejs

cd console && npm ci && npm run build   # → console/dist

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio

# amd64 — ISA-L on
cargo build --workspace --release --features isal

# arm64 — pure-Rust EC
cargo build --workspace --release

Binaries land in target/release/. For a system install:

sudo install -m 0755 target/release/objectio-{aio,gateway,meta,osd,cli,install,block-gateway} \
  /usr/local/bin/

Then proceed as in section 2.

docs.title: Run the test suite
docs.text:
cargo test --workspace --features isal
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features isal -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all -- --check
# Or the one-shot:
make ci

docs.title: Disk preparation — production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Dedicate whole disks to OSDs (no partitioning, no filesystem).
  • [ ] Disable write-cache on SAS/SATA drives with non-battery-backed controllers: hdparm -W 0 /dev/sdX.
  • [ ] For NVMe, confirm the drive supports FUA (Force Unit Access) — check nvme id-ctrl -H <dev> | grep -i fua.
  • [ ] Raise /proc/sys/fs/file-max and ulimit -n (OSD opens one fd per concurrent operation × disk).
  • [ ] Pin CPUs / set tuned-adm profile throughput-performance.
  • [ ] If using io_uring, make sure the kernel is 5.15+ and /proc/sys/kernel/io_uring_disabled is 0.

See topologies.md for how many disks and nodes to size for a given durability target.

docs.title: systemd unit reference
docs.text:
objectio-install --systemd installs standard units. If you're bootstrapping manually, here's the skeleton for the OSD (the others are analogous — replace paths and drop the CAP_SYS_RAWIO bits for non-OSD roles):

# /etc/systemd/system/objectio-osd.service
[Unit]
Description=ObjectIO Object Storage Daemon
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
# OSD needs raw-disk access. Use CAP_SYS_RAWIO rather than running as root.
User=objectio
Group=objectio
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_SYS_RAWIO
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_SYS_RAWIO
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/objectio-osd --config /etc/objectio/osd.toml
Restart=always
RestartSec=5
LimitNOFILE=1048576
# Durability: kill -9 only after giving the OSD time to checkpoint
TimeoutStopSec=60

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

For the gateway and meta services, drop CAP_SYS_RAWIO and keep the same shape.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
sudo systemctl disable --now objectio-gateway objectio-meta objectio-osd
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/objectio-{gateway,meta,osd}.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo rm /usr/local/bin/objectio-*
# Data + config (destructive):
sudo rm -rf /etc/objectio /var/lib/objectio /var/log/objectio
sudo userdel objectio && sudo groupdel objectio

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
macOS is a development-and-test target, not a production target. Use it to build, run objectio-aio, and point Spark / PyIceberg / boto3 at a local S3 endpoint. The split-service OSD binary runs on macOS, but Darwin does not expose the same raw-disk semantics as Linux (O_DIRECT, ioctl BLKGETSIZE64) and the storage engine has no hardened path for APFS-backed OSD disks. Keep macOS deployments to AIO mode or a Docker-hosted cluster.

Both Apple Silicon (arm64) and Intel (x86_64) are supported. Erasure coding uses the pure-Rust SIMD backend on arm64 and ISA-L on x86_64; wire format is identical.

docs.title: 1. AIO binary (recommended)
docs.text: This is the fastest path and the one you'll actually want 95% of the time on macOS.

docs.title: Apple Silicon
docs.text:
curl -L -o objectio-aio \
  https://github.com/object-io/objectio/releases/latest/download/objectio-aio-darwin-arm64
chmod +x objectio-aio && sudo mv objectio-aio /usr/local/bin/

docs.title: Intel
docs.text:
curl -L -o objectio-aio \
  https://github.com/object-io/objectio/releases/latest/download/objectio-aio-darwin-amd64
chmod +x objectio-aio && sudo mv objectio-aio /usr/local/bin/

docs.title: Gatekeeper
docs.text:
Unsigned release binaries will be quarantined by Gatekeeper on first run. Either remove the quarantine attribute:

xattr -d com.apple.quarantine /usr/local/bin/objectio-aio

or, on the first launch, open System Settings → Privacy & Security and click Allow Anyway next to the objectio-aio entry.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
objectio-aio --data "$HOME/.objectio"

Banner prints the admin AK/SK. --data is optional but recommended — without it, every restart wipes the data tempdir.

docs.title: 2. Docker Desktop (AIO container)
docs.text:
If you already have Docker Desktop and want zero host install:

docker run --rm -p 9000:9000 \
  -v objectio-data:/var/lib/objectio \
  ghcr.io/object-io/objectio:latest objectio-aio --data /var/lib/objectio

On Apple Silicon, Docker Desktop pulls the linux/arm64 image automatically — EC falls back to pure Rust (no emulation). On Intel, you get the ISA-L path.

For the full 10-container compose cluster (3 meta + 6 OSD + 1 gateway), see docker.md.

docs.title: 3. Build from source (contributor path)
docs.text: Only needed if you're hacking on ObjectIO itself.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text:
# Rust
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
rustup toolchain install 1.93

# Build deps via Homebrew
brew install nasm autoconf automake libtool llvm protobuf cmake

# Node 22+ for the console SPA (only if you need /_console/)
brew install node@22

nasm is Intel-only (drives ISA-L assembly). On Apple Silicon, Homebrew still installs it and the build script ignores it.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio

# Apple Silicon — pure-Rust EC (ISA-L is x86-only)
cargo build --workspace --release

# Intel — ISA-L
cargo build --workspace --release --features isal

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
If you want the React /_console/ UI baked into objectio-aio:

cd console && npm ci && npm run build
cd .. && cargo build --workspace --release    # rebuild to embed dist

docs.title: Run
docs.text: ./target/release/objectio-aio --data "$HOME/.objectio"

docs.title: What does not work on macOS
docs.text:
• Production OSDs on raw disks. Darwin's /dev/disk* devices don't support the same O_DIRECT / BLKGETSIZE64 interface the storage engine uses. The OSD binary builds and runs against file- backed "disks" (truncate -s 10G disk0.raw), which is fine for unit tests but not for durability-sensitive work.
  • NBD / block-gateway targets. The block gateway terminates iSCSI / NBD from Linux initiators; macOS has no native initiator for either. Use Linux peers for block-storage testing.
  • io_uring performance path. Linux-specific. Not a correctness issue, but macOS performance numbers are not representative.

For any of these, run ObjectIO in a Linux VM (Lima, UTM, Colima, Docker Desktop's Linux VM, or a dedicated machine).

docs.title: Typical dev loop on macOS
docs.text:
# 1. Run AIO in one terminal, persistent data dir
objectio-aio --data "$HOME/.objectio"

# 2. Point your tool at it
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...  # printed in the AIO banner
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000

# 3. Work against S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing
aws s3 ls
curl -s http://localhost:9000/iceberg/v1/config | jq .

# 4. Console (browser)
open http://localhost:9000/_console/

Shut down with Ctrl-C — AIO drains cleanly. The data directory is reusable across restarts.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
The fastest path to a running ObjectIO is the all-in-one binary (objectio-aio). It runs meta + OSD + gateway as tokio tasks in a single process, shares one log stream, and is shut down with a single Ctrl-C. Same wire protocol as a real cluster — what's different is that there is no HA and no redundancy by default.

This page covers the three fastest paths:

Path Platform Best for AIO binary Linux, macOS Laptop-local S3/Iceberg/Delta endpoint AIO container Linux, macOS Quick CI or demo; no host Rust toolchain make cluster-up Linux, macOS Real 3-meta + 6-OSD + gateway topology with 4+2 EC

ObjectIO is POSIX-only — no native Windows build. The storage engine uses O_DIRECT, ioctl BLKGETSIZE64, and other unix-only interfaces; there is no meaningful cfg-gate to Windows.

For a production walkthrough, jump to Linux · macOS · Docker · Kubernetes.

docs.title: 1. AIO binary (fastest — no Docker)
docs.text: Downloads a single pre-built binary from the latest GitHub release and runs it. No background services, no daemons, data in a tempdir unless you say otherwise.

docs.title: macOS (Apple Silicon)
docs.text:
curl -L -o objectio-aio \
  https://github.com/object-io/objectio/releases/latest/download/objectio-aio-darwin-arm64
chmod +x objectio-aio && sudo mv objectio-aio /usr/local/bin/
objectio-aio

docs.title: macOS (Intel)
docs.text:
curl -L -o objectio-aio \
  https://github.com/object-io/objectio/releases/latest/download/objectio-aio-darwin-amd64
chmod +x objectio-aio && sudo mv objectio-aio /usr/local/bin/
objectio-aio

docs.title: Linux (x86_64, with ISA-L acceleration)
docs.text:
curl -L -o objectio-aio \
  https://github.com/object-io/objectio/releases/latest/download/objectio-aio-linux-amd64
chmod +x objectio-aio && sudo mv objectio-aio /usr/local/bin/
objectio-aio

docs.title: Linux (aarch64 / Raspberry Pi 5, pure-Rust EC)
docs.text:
curl -L -o objectio-aio \
  https://github.com/object-io/objectio/releases/latest/download/objectio-aio-linux-arm64
chmod +x objectio-aio && sudo mv objectio-aio /usr/local/bin/
objectio-aio

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
On start, AIO prints its admin AK/SK and a ready-to-paste aws command:

┌─ ObjectIO ready ──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing:  http://localhost:9000          │
│ Console:                       http://localhost:9000/_console │
│                                                               │
│ AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=OBJIO…                                      │
│ AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=…                                       │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Smoke test from another terminal:

export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...   # from the banner above
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 mb s3://demo
echo 'hello objectio' | aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 cp - s3://demo/hello.txt
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 cp s3://demo/hello.txt -

docs.title: Flags you'll actually use
docs.text:
Flag Default Notes --port 9000 Public port. Only port the caller needs to know. --listen-addr 0.0.0.0 Use 127.0.0.1 to restrict to loopback. --data <dir> tempdir Persist data across restarts. Creates meta/, osd-N/, admin-creds.env. --osds <N> 1 Set to 3 to run 2+1 EC inside a single process. --strict-port off Fail fast on --port conflict instead of picking an ephemeral.

Full objectio-aio --help for the complete surface.

docs.title: 2. AIO container (no host toolchain, no host binary)
docs.text: The objectio image ("AIO" / all-in-one target) packages every binary plus the console SPA. Good for CI, demos, and any box where you don't want to install anything local.

docs.title: Pre-built image
docs.text:
docker run --rm -p 9000:9000 \
  -v objectio-data:/var/lib/objectio \
  ghcr.io/object-io/objectio:latest objectio-aio --data /var/lib/objectio

docs.title: Build locally
docs.text:
If the image isn't published yet (or you want the current main):

git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio
docker build --target all -t objectio:local .
docker run --rm -p 9000:9000 objectio:local objectio-aio

The AIO image bundles objectio-gateway, objectio-meta, objectio-osd, obioctl, objectio-install, and objectio-block-gateway — you pick the entrypoint per run.

ARM64 (Apple Silicon, Graviton, Raspberry Pi) runs the pure-Rust EC backend automatically; x86_64 gets ISA-L hardware acceleration. The wire format is identical — mixing arches in a cluster is fine.

docs.title: 3. Real local cluster (3 meta, 6 OSDs, 4+2 EC)
docs.text:
For a more production-shaped setup, use the Makefile helper. It builds every image and starts deploy/local-cluster/docker-compose.yml:

git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio
make cluster-up            # builds images, starts the stack

make cluster-status        # check that all 10 containers are Up
make cluster-logs          # tail everything
make cluster-logs-gateway  # just the gateway
make cluster-down          # stop, keep volumes
make cluster-clean         # stop, wipe volumes

S3 endpoint stays at http://localhost:9000. Data is persisted in Docker volumes (cluster-clean to wipe).

Same smoke test works:

aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 mb s3://demo

See docker.md for what's inside the compose file, how to point it at raw disks (deploy/prod/), and how to layer on the Prometheus + Grafana stack.

docs.title: Deployment Topologies
docs.text: ObjectIO supports various deployment configurations. For worked scenarios, configuration examples and capacity planning, see deployment-options.md.

docs.title: Topology 1: Single-Node Multi-Disk
docs.text:
Best for development, edge, and small deployments.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Single Server                      │
│                                                     │
│  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐        │
│  │ Disk 1 │ │ Disk 2 │ │ Disk 3 │ │ Disk 4 │ ...    │
│  │ Shard1 │ │ Shard2 │ │ Shard3 │ │ Shard4 │        │
│  └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘        │
│                                                     │
│  EC 4+2: Spread 6 shards across 6+ disks            │
│                                                     │
│  Components:                                        │
│  • objectio-gateway (port 9000)                     │
│  • objectio-meta (embedded, single-node mode)       │
│  • objectio-osd (manages all disks)                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Characteristics: - Survives: Disk failures (up to m disks) - Does NOT survive: Server failure - Storage efficiency: 67% (4+2)

Example Configuration:

# docker-compose.single-node.yml
services:
  objectio:
    image: objectio:latest
    ports:
      - "9000:9000"
    volumes:
      - /dev/vdb:/dev/vdb
      - /dev/vdc:/dev/vdc
      - /dev/vdd:/dev/vdd
      - /dev/vde:/dev/vde
      - /dev/vdf:/dev/vdf
      - /dev/vdg:/dev/vdg
    privileged: true

docs.title: Topology 3: Multi-DC / Multi-AZ
docs.text:
Geo-distributed deployment for disaster recovery.

┌───────────────────────┐    ┌───────────────────────┐    ┌───────────────────────┐
│    Datacenter 1       │    │    Datacenter 2       │    │    Datacenter 3       │
│    (Primary)          │    │    (Secondary)        │    │    (DR)               │
│                       │    │                       │    │                       │
│  ┌─────────────────┐  │    │  ┌─────────────────┐  │    │  ┌─────────────────┐  │
│  │   Full Copy 1   │  │    │  │   Full Copy 2   │  │    │  │   Full Copy 3   │  │
│  │   (EC within)   │◄─┼────┼─►│   (EC within)   │◄─┼────┼─►│   (EC within)   │  │
│  └─────────────────┘  │    │  └─────────────────┘  │    │  └─────────────────┘  │
│         │             │    │         │             │    │         │             │
│    ┌────┴────┐        │    │    ┌────┴────┐        │    │    ┌────┴────┐        │
│    │Racks/   │        │    │    │Racks/   │        │    │    │Racks/   │        │
│    │Nodes    │        │    │    │Nodes    │        │    │    │Nodes    │        │
│    └─────────┘        │    │    └─────────┘        │    │    └─────────┘        │
│                       │    │                       │    │                       │
│  Metadata: Local Raft │    │  Metadata: Local Raft │    │  Metadata: Local Raft │
└───────────────────────┘    └───────────────────────┘    └───────────────────────┘
         │                            │                            │
         └────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┘
                                      │
                            Async Replication

Data Flow: 1. Write arrives at DC1 gateway 2. EC encode + write to DC1 storage nodes 3. Async replicate full object to DC2, DC3 4. Read can be served from any DC

Characteristics: - Survives: Complete DC/AZ failure (up to 2 DCs with 3x replication) - Use case: Geo-distributed, disaster recovery, compliance

Configuration:

storage_class:
  type: hybrid
  local_protection:
    type: erasure_coding
    ec_profile: "4+2"
    placement: rack
  geo_protection:
    type: replication
    replicas: 3
    sync_mode: async

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Topology Failure Tolerance Complexity Use Case Single-node Disk only Low Dev, edge Multi-node Disk, node, rack Medium Production Multi-DC Disk, node, rack, DC High Multi-site production

docs.title: Single-Node Multi-Disk
docs.text: Choose if: - Development or testing - Edge deployment with limited hardware - Cost-sensitive deployments - Acceptable single-node failure risk

docs.title: Multi-Node Single-DC
docs.text: Choose if: - Production workloads - Node and rack fault tolerance required - Single datacenter deployment - No geo-redundancy needs

docs.title: Multi-DC / Multi-AZ
docs.text: Choose if: - Business-critical data - Regulatory compliance (data locality) - Disaster recovery requirements - Global distribution needed

docs.text:
# Start all services
sudo systemctl start objectio-gateway objectio-meta objectio-osd

# Stop all services
sudo systemctl stop objectio-gateway objectio-meta objectio-osd

# Restart a specific service
sudo systemctl restart objectio-gateway

# Check service status
sudo systemctl status objectio-gateway

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
# Gateway health
curl http://localhost:9000/health

# Check cluster status via CLI
obioctl cluster info

# Check OSD status
obioctl node list

docs.title: Common Operations
docs.text: Task Command List buckets obioctl bucket list Check capacity and usage obioctl cluster usage, obioctl node show <osd-id> View cluster map obioctl cluster topology Check repair obioctl metrics query 'objectio_objects_at_risk' (repair is continuous) Drain OSD obioctl osd set-state <osd-id> draining, then obioctl cluster drain-status

docs.title: Rolling Upgrades
docs.text:
1. Upgrade OSDs first, one at a time. Don't drain them: a drain moves all of an OSD's data, and a restart doesn't need it — 4+2 serves reads and writes with an OSD briefly down. 

    sudo systemctl stop objectio-osd@osd1
# ... upgrade binary ...
sudo systemctl start objectio-osd@osd1

# Before the next one: nothing one failure from unreadable
obioctl metrics query 'objectio_objects_at_risk'     # expect 0

  2. Upgrade metadata nodes (one at a time): 

    # Check which node is leader
curl -s http://meta1:9102/status

# Upgrade followers first, leader last
sudo systemctl restart objectio-meta@meta2
sudo systemctl restart objectio-meta@meta3
sudo systemctl restart objectio-meta@meta1  # leader

  3. Upgrade gateways (one at a time): 

    sudo systemctl restart objectio-gateway

docs.title: Adding Capacity
docs.text:
Start an OSD on the new host; it registers itself with meta and joins placement. Placement groups rebalance onto it in the background:

obioctl node list                 # the new OSD, "in"
obioctl cluster rebalance status

docs.title: Removing an OSD
docs.text:
obioctl osd set-state <osd-id> draining     # copies everything off it
obioctl cluster drain-status                # until it is "out"

When the drain finishes the OSD is marked out and wiped. Then stop it and take the hardware away.

docs.title: Metadata Backup
docs.text:
Raft log + state are persisted in each meta pod's redb database on its PVC. Log compaction (snapshotting) is on the Raft roadmap; until then logs grow without bound on long-lived clusters, so periodically back up the PVC contents:

# Snapshot each meta pod's PVC (use your storage class's snapshot
# mechanism — VolumeSnapshot API, CSI snapshotter, etc.)
kubectl get pvc -n objectio -l app.kubernetes.io/component=meta

# For disaster recovery, restore the PVCs before redeploying — a fresh
# helm install against empty PVCs starts a new cluster with no
# history.

docs.title: Object Recovery
docs.text: Repair is continuous: any stripe with at least k readable shards is rebuilt automatically. An object below k shards can't be recovered by any command; objectio_meta_repair_unrecoverable_stripes_total counts them.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Quick Reference
docs.text: Symptom Check Solution Slow uploads Network, OSD load Scale gateways, add OSDs High latency Metadata service Check Raft leader via curl meta-N:9102/status, disk I/O Objects missing OSD health objectio_objects_at_risk, objectio_meta_repair_unrecoverable_stripes_total Auth failures User credentials Verify access keys Connection refused Service status Restart services

docs.title: Complete Cluster Recovery
docs.text:
If all metadata nodes fail but their PVCs survive:

  1. kubectl rollout restart statefulset/objectio-meta — each pod restarts, reads its persisted Raft log from redb, and re-joins. openraft handles log alignment and re-election automatically.
  2. OSDs + gateways keep running throughout.

If the PVCs are lost (unrecoverable storage-layer failure):

  1. Restore PVCs from the latest snapshot if you have one.
  2. Otherwise: kubectl delete statefulset/objectio-meta + PVCs, then helm upgrade — the post-install Job bootstraps a fresh cluster. Pre-Raft cluster state is lost; tenants, users, buckets, etc. need to be recreated.

docs.title: Data Recovery from Raw Disks
docs.text:
Not available: object metadata lives on the OSDs and meta's Raft log, but there is no tool yet to rebuild a cluster's metadata from raw disks. Keep meta's PVCs snapshotted (above).

See Failure Recovery for detailed recovery procedures.

docs.title: Failure Recovery
docs.text: Handling failures in ObjectIO clusters.

docs.title: Failure Domains
docs.text:
ObjectIO is designed to tolerate failures at multiple levels:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Failure Domain Hierarchy                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Datacenter ──┬── Rack ──┬── Host ──┬── Disk                    │
│               │          │          │                           │
│               │          │          └── Single disk failure     │
│               │          │              (most common)           │
│               │          │                                      │
│               │          └── Node failure                       │
│               │              (power, OS, hardware)              │
│               │                                                 │
│               └── Rack failure                                  │
│                   (power, network switch)                       │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Detection
docs.text: OSDs detect disk failures via: - I/O errors during read/write - SMART monitoring (if enabled) - Scrubbing (background verification)

docs.title: Automatic Recovery
docs.text:
With 4+2 erasure coding, the cluster tolerates 2 disk failures:

Object: photo.jpg (split into 6 shards)

Before failure:
  Disk1: shard1 ✓    Disk4: shard4 ✓
  Disk2: shard2 ✓    Disk5: shard5 ✓
  Disk3: shard3 ✓    Disk6: shard6 ✓

After Disk3 fails:
  Disk1: shard1 ✓    Disk4: shard4 ✓
  Disk2: shard2 ✓    Disk5: shard5 ✓
  Disk3: shard3 ✗    Disk6: shard6 ✓

Recovery: shard3 reconstructed from any 4 remaining shards
          → placed on spare disk (Disk7)

docs.title: Replacing a disk
docs.text:
Lost shards are rebuilt automatically: the repairer in meta finds stripes missing a shard and rebuilds it on another OSD. Watch it work:

obioctl metrics query 'objectio_objects_at_risk'        # objects one more loss from unreadable
obioctl metrics query 'objectio_degraded_bytes'
obioctl metrics query 'rate(objectio_meta_repair_shards_rebuilt_total[5m])'
obioctl metrics query 'objectio_meta_repair_unrecoverable_stripes_total'

To take an OSD's disk out of service (still readable):

obioctl node list                               # find the OSD's id
obioctl osd set-state <osd-id> draining         # copies everything off it
obioctl cluster drain-status                    # progress; it turns "out" when done

When a drain finishes, the OSD is marked out and wiped (its space is reclaimed, and nothing stale can come back with it). Replace the hardware, start the OSD on the new disk, and set it back in:

obioctl osd set-state <osd-id> in

For a disk that is already dead, set its OSD out straight away; repair rebuilds its shards from the others. Don't put a directly-out OSD back in with old data on it: wipe the disk first.

docs.title: Full disks
docs.text:
Client writes may fill each OSD disk up to its full ratio (--full-ratio, default 0.95, as Ceph's full_ratio). Past that:

  • Writes are refused with 507 StorageFull when a shard's OSD has no room under its ratio and the write can't reach its quorum without it. S3 clients don't retry a 507 blindly, as they would a 503.
  • The rest of the disk is kept for writes that restore redundancy: repair, drain and backfill set use_reserve on their shard writes. A shard lost on a full cluster can still be rebuilt.
  • Nothing acknowledged is lost, and reads and deletes go on.
  • Deleting frees the space, and writes are admitted again.

Watch for it before it happens. Alert when an OSD passes about 85%:

objectio_osd_used_bytes / objectio_osd_capacity_bytes > 0.85

Then add OSDs or a pool, or delete data. Tested by the full_disk e2e suite: a 4+2 cluster on 1 GiB disks is filled with 4 MiB objects until writes are refused. The refusals are StorageFull, no OSD passes about 95%, the acknowledged objects read back intact, and deleting half lets writes in again.

docs.title: Types of OSD Failures
docs.text: Type Detection Impact Process crash Heartbeat timeout Temporary unavailability Network partition Heartbeat timeout Partial cluster access Hardware failure No heartbeat Requires repair

docs.title: Recovery Process
docs.text:
1. Meta probes every OSD every 15 s (every 2 s just after it starts); three misses in a row (about 45 s) mark it Down.
  2. A Down OSD keeps its placement positions. Writes go on at k + 1 shards (degraded), and reads decode around it. Its shards are not rebuilt elsewhere: it may come back, and moving them would cost more than waiting.
  3. When it comes back, repair rebuilds only the shards written while it was gone.
  4. When it is set out (obioctl osd set-state <node_id> out: the host or drive is gone for good), its positions move to other OSDs, and repair rebuilds its shards there from the rest of each stripe.

Setting a dead OSD out is the operator's decision; nothing does it automatically. See the production runbooks.

docs.title: Manual Recovery
docs.text:
obioctl node list                  # status and admin state of every OSD
obioctl node show <osd-id>         # its disks and capacity
obioctl cluster topology           # where it sits in the failure domains
obioctl metrics query 'objectio_meta_repair_last_pass_timestamp_seconds'

Repair is continuous; there is nothing to start by hand. An OSD that is down long enough to be replaced should be set out (see above).

docs.title: Restarting a Failed OSD
docs.text:
# Check logs for failure reason
journalctl -u objectio-osd@osd3 -n 100

# Common issues:
# - Disk I/O errors → check disk health
# - Out of memory → increase limits or add RAM
# - Network issues → check connectivity

# Restart OSD
sudo systemctl restart objectio-osd@osd3

# Verify reconnection
obioctl node show osd3

docs.title: Raft consensus (openraft 0.9)
docs.text:
The metadata service runs openraft. Every meta pod is a Raft member; cluster size is a deployment decision via meta.replicas in the helm chart:

meta.replicas Semantics Survives 1 Single-voter cluster Pod restart with PVC intact 3 3-voter quorum 1 pod loss 5 5-voter quorum 2 pod losses

Phase R1 routes cluster config mutations (SetConfig / DeleteConfig) through the Raft log. Other mutations (users, buckets, tenants, etc.) still write to redb directly pending the R2+ migration — those are quorum-safe only because they're leader-only in practice.

docs.title: Admin API
docs.text:
All endpoints are plain HTTP on the meta admin port (default 9102). They're meta-local and not exposed via the gateway.

# Cluster state (leader id, term, voters, learners, last_log_index)
curl http://meta-0:9102/status | jq

# Force a node into the cluster as a learner (non-voting, catches up
# via log replication):
curl -X POST http://meta-0:9102/add-learner \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"node_id": 4, "addr": "meta-3.meta-headless:9100"}'

# Promote learners to voters (pass the full voter list, not a delta):
curl -X POST http://meta-0:9102/change-membership \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"voters": [1,2,3,4]}'

docs.title: Single pod failure in a 3-node cluster
docs.text:
Cluster continues with 2/3 nodes. Election is automatic; the old leader's clients see failed_precondition "not the raft leader — forward to node X" on the next write and retry there.

# Simulate a leader crash. Use `--grace-period=0 --force` — a graceful
# shutdown keeps sending heartbeats during the termination window,
# which suppresses the follower election until the container actually
# exits:
kubectl delete pod -n objectio objectio-meta-0 --grace-period=0 --force

# Watch followers elect a new leader (expect ~5s from kill to new
# leader with default heartbeat=250ms, election_timeout=500–1000ms,
# leader_lease=1s):
for i in 1 2; do
  curl -s http://objectio-meta-$i.objectio-meta-headless:9102/status
done

Verified on a kind cluster (2026-04-18): leader (node 1) force-deleted at T+0s; meta-1 (node 2) became leader at term=2, log index 6 at ~T+5s. Meta-2 recognized the new leader in the same interval. Writes continued against the new leader. When meta-0's StatefulSet pod came back on its existing PVC ~30s later, it read its Raft log, noticed the higher term, stepped down from its stored leader state, received AppendEntries from the new leader, and rejoined as Follower at term=2/log=6 without operator action.

Bootstrap addresses matter. The membership stores the peer advertise address. Bootstrap must use the new helm chart (which sets --raft-advertise $HOSTNAME.objectio-meta-headless:9100) — a kubectl set image rollover on a pre-Raft StatefulSet misses the new args and would register node 1 with listen address 0.0.0.0:9100, breaking future replication to that pod. Re-install fresh when rolling up from a pre-R1 release.

docs.title: Complete metadata cluster failure
docs.text:
Scenario: all meta pods lose their PVCs simultaneously (rare — typically requires a storage-layer incident).

# If all pods still have their PVCs, just wait — each pod's redb log
# is durable, so restarting the StatefulSet recovers the cluster.
kubectl rollout restart statefulset/objectio-meta -n objectio

# If PVCs are lost, the cluster is lost — there's no quorum to recover
# from. Treat it like a fresh install:
kubectl delete statefulset/objectio-meta pvc -l app.kubernetes.io/component=meta
helm upgrade objectio ./deploy/helm/objectio -f values.yaml
# Helm's post-install Job re-runs /init + /add-learner + /change-membership
# against the new meta-0.

docs.title: Network partitions
docs.text:
Raft's quorum requirement prevents split-brain. In a 3-node cluster partitioned 1 + 2:

  • Minority side (1 pod): can't elect a leader, refuses writes with RaftError::Fatal("not ready").
  • Majority side (2 pods): re-elects a leader if the old one was on the minority side; continues serving writes.

When the partition heals, the minority catches up via AppendEntries and resumes as follower. No manual intervention needed.

docs.title: Stateless Recovery
docs.text:
Gateways are stateless - simply restart:

sudo systemctl restart objectio-gateway

docs.title: Load Balancer Health Checks
docs.text:
Configure health checks in your load balancer:

# nginx example
upstream objectio {
    server gateway1:9000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
    server gateway2:9000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
}

server {
    location /health {
        proxy_pass http://objectio/health;
    }
}

docs.title: Network Partitions
docs.text: Meta-side partition behavior is covered in the Metadata Service Failures section above. Gateway/OSD partitions are handled by client-side retry.

docs.title: Client Retry Logic
docs.text:
Clients should retry on different gateways:

import boto3
from botocore.config import Config

# Configure retries
config = Config(
    retries={
        'max_attempts': 3,
        'mode': 'adaptive'
    }
)

s3 = boto3.client('s3', config=config)

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
• Online: CRC32C verification on every read
  • Offline: Background scrubbing

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: A read that finds a shard failing its checksum decodes the object from the other shards and returns correct data; the scrubber and the repairer rebuild the bad shard. There is no manual step. Watch objectio_meta_repair_shards_rebuilt_total and objectio_meta_repair_unrecoverable_stripes_total (should stay 0).

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: Meta is a Raft group (3+ nodes) and survives the loss of a minority. To protect against losing the whole cluster, copy data to another one with an S3 tool (rclone sync, aws s3 sync) on a schedule. Built-in cross-site replication is planned, not available.

docs.title: Recovery Time Objectives
docs.text: Failure Type RTO RPO Single disk Automatic 0 (no data loss) Single OSD Automatic 0 (no data loss) Single metadata node < 5 seconds 0 Loss of a meta majority Until a majority is back 0 (Raft log) Complete cluster loss Restore from your copy Last copy

docs.title: Failure Simulation
docs.text: Test recovery in a staging cluster by failing things for real: stop an OSD process (systemctl stop objectio-osd@osd3), detach a disk, or partition a meta node with a firewall rule. Then check that objectio_objects_at_risk returns to 0 and that a checksum-verified read of a sample of objects (aws s3 cp and compare) succeeds. The end-to-end tests in the source tree (tests/e2e/tests/{repair,drain}.rs) do exactly this against objectio-aio.

docs.title: Meta high availability
docs.text: Meta runs as a Raft group, normally three nodes. A group of three keeps serving while any two are up; five, while any three are.

docs.title: What clients need
docs.text:
Give every gateway, OSD and block gateway every meta node's address, comma-separated:

--meta-endpoint http://meta1:9100,http://meta2:9100,http://meta3:9100

In Kubernetes, the chart's meta Service does the same job: point clients at it.

  • Any meta node serves any call. A follower forwards the call to the Raft leader and relays the answer, so clients never see a follower's possibly stale state, and never need to know which node leads.
  • A node that stops answering is skipped. Clients probe each meta address every second, with a one-second timeout, and leave out the ones that don't answer until they do. That covers a node that is down, and one that is frozen or cut off but still accepting connections.
  • No call waits forever. A call to meta gives up after 5 seconds. The gateway answers S3 clients 503 when meta can't be reached, which they retry.

docs.title: What happens when a meta node is lost
docs.text: Lost Effect A follower Nothing visible. Calls in flight to it fail and are retried; new calls go to the others. When it returns it catches up from the leader. The leader The others elect a new leader within a second or two. Writes resume within a few seconds; calls in flight at the moment of loss fail (503) and are retried. No acknowledged write is lost. The leader, cut off (frozen, partitioned) As above. When it returns it finds a newer term and steps down: it never leads a second cluster. A majority Writes are refused (503) rather than accepted without a quorum. Service resumes as soon as a majority is back, with nothing acknowledged lost.

docs.title: What is replicated
docs.text:
Everything clients rely on lives in the Raft log, so a new leader has it: buckets, users and keys (including the bootstrap admin), policies, tenants, pools, placement groups, the shared-stripe registry, packs, block volumes and chunks, OSD registrations, KMS keys, and multipart uploads in progress.

The bootstrap admin is created once for the cluster, by the first leader; every meta node writes the same admin-creds.env.

docs.title: Log compaction
docs.text: The Raft log doesn't grow without bound. Every --raft-snapshot-every entries (default 500,000), each meta node writes a snapshot of its state and drops the log up to it, keeping the last --raft-keep-logs entries (default 10,000). A node that falls further behind, or a new node, is sent a snapshot of the whole metadata database. It travels in chunks and goes through <data-dir>/raft-snapshots/, so leave free space there of about the size of meta.redb. /status on the admin port shows how far the last snapshot (snapshot) and the purge (purged) reach.

docs.title: Replacing a meta node
docs.text:
Use the Raft admin API on the leader (port 9102 by default):

# 1. Start the new node (empty data dir, a new --node-id), then add it.
curl -X POST meta1:9102/add-learner -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"node_id": 4, "addr": "meta4:9100"}'
# 2. Make the voters the surviving nodes plus the new one.
curl -X POST meta1:9102/change-membership -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"voters": [1, 2, 4]}'
# 3. Stop the old node and remove its data.
curl meta1:9102/status   # voters, leader, last applied index

Add the new node's address to clients' --meta-endpoint.

docs.title: How it's tested
docs.text:
tests/e2e/tests/meta_ha.rs runs three meta nodes, six OSDs and two gateways as separate processes, with writers running through both gateways:

  • the leader killed: writes resume within seconds, and every acknowledged write reads back through both gateways;
  • a follower killed and restarted: it catches up, then the leader is killed and the cluster carries on;
  • the leader frozen (SIGSTOP): a new leader is elected, and the old one steps down when it thaws;
  • two of three lost: writes refused, then resumed when one returns;
  • a KMS key, the objects encrypted under it, a multipart upload in progress, and the admin's credentials all survive a failover;
  • a meta node replaced by a new, empty one, which then forms part of the majority when another is lost.

docs.title: Metrics reference
docs.text:
Every Prometheus metric ObjectIO exports: where it comes from, what it means, and the alerts worth setting on it. For dashboards, Prometheus setup and the console's views of these metrics, see Monitoring.

All metrics are plain Prometheus text exposition. Names start with objectio_ (and process_ for the standard process family).

docs.title: Where to scrape
docs.text:
Process Endpoint Notes Gateway :9000/metrics Or the --admin-listen address when the admin surface is split off. Meta :9101/metrics --metrics-port; 0 serves none. OSD :9201/metrics --metrics-port; 0 serves none. Block gateway :9301/metrics --metrics-listen; empty serves none.

One gateway (and aio): scrape the gateway alone. By default the gateway polls every OSD and meta node every 30 seconds and re-exports their metrics on its own /metrics. Re-exported OSD series carry an osd_id label, and meta series carry component="meta". The all-in-one binary runs meta, the OSDs and the block gateway in one process with their own ports off, so the gateway's /metrics is the only endpoint and carries everything.

Several gateways (the helm chart): scrape every process directly. Run gateways with --no-reexport-metrics (the chart does, via gateway.reexportMetrics: false). Otherwise each gateway exports a copy of every OSD's and meta's metrics, and every sum multiplies by the number of gateways. The chart's Prometheus scrapes meta on 9101 and the OSDs on 9201 directly.

Do not do both. Scraping a re-exporting gateway and the OSDs and meta directly counts every OSD and meta series twice.

Series the gateway derives from its own poll (objectio_cluster_*, objectio_osd_capacity_bytes, the usage and data-safety families) exist once per gateway. With several gateways, aggregate them with max, not sum.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Latency is a histogram, in seconds, with buckets from 1 ms to 10 s (or wider where noted). Take percentiles with histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(<name>_bucket[5m]))), and keep le in any sum by.
  • Counters reset when a process restarts. Use rate() or increase(), which handle resets.
  • A family can be absent. Counter and histogram families appear once something has been recorded. SMART families need smartctl on the host. Iceberg, Unity, lifecycle and drain families need those features in use. Absent is not the same as zero.
  • Label cardinality is bounded. Operations, methods, codes and reasons come from fixed sets. Per-bucket usage (objectio_bucket_*) is one series per bucket; leave it out with --no-bucket-metrics past tens of thousands of buckets. Per-volume and per-snapshot series are one per volume and snapshot.
  • gRPC status codes use gRPC's names (OK, NOT_FOUND, UNAVAILABLE…). A streaming call that fails part-way counts as OK; its status arrives after the response headers, where it is measured.
