docs.title: Alerts
docs.text: The chart ships the alert rules (deploy/helm/objectio/alerts/objectio-rules.yaml in the code repo). Production lists them, with a runbook for each.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• Gateway to meta calls are measured only on meta's side (objectio_meta_grpc_latency_seconds), which leaves out network time.
  • Lifecycle expiry deletes an object's metadata but not its shards (a known leak); objectio_lifecycle_actions_total{action="expire"} counts the deletes, and the space they leave is not reclaimed yet.
  • The Transfer Engine (RDMA) path reports transfers and fallbacks, but not its own latency.
  • Tracing (OpenTelemetry spans across gateway, meta and OSD) is not implemented.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: How to watch an ObjectIO cluster: where its metrics are, how to have Prometheus collect them, the dashboards and console views built on them, and the health endpoints. Every metric, its labels and the alerts worth setting on it are in the metrics reference.

docs.title: What exports metrics
docs.text:
Process Metrics endpoint Health Gateway :9000/metrics (or --admin-listen) /health, /_ready Meta :9101/metrics (--metrics-port, 0 = off) :9101/health OSD :9201/metrics (--metrics-port, 0 = off) :9201/health Block gateway :9301/metrics (--metrics-listen, empty = off) —

By default the gateway also re-exports the OSDs' and meta's metrics, which it polls every 30 seconds. That way one scrape target covers a small cluster: aio, or a single gateway. With several gateways that duplicates every series, so turn it off with --no-reexport-metrics and scrape each process directly. The metrics reference explains the choice.

docs.title: aio
docs.text:
objectio-aio runs meta, the OSDs, the gateway and (with --block-port) the block gateway in one process. Their own metrics ports are off and everything is on the gateway's /metrics:

curl -s http://localhost:9000/metrics | grep objectio_meta_raft_is_leader

A Prometheus scrape config for it:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: objectio
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9000']

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
The chart runs gateways with --no-reexport-metrics (gateway.reexportMetrics: false). With monitoring.enabled, it deploys a Prometheus that discovers and scrapes the gateway service (:9000), each meta pod (:9101) and each OSD pod (:9201). For a Prometheus of your own, scrape those three the same way: every gateway pod, every meta pod, every OSD pod.

Turn gateway.reexportMetrics on only for a single gateway scraped on its own.

docs.title: Prometheus and the console
docs.text:
The console (/_console/) charts these metrics under Monitoring:

Tab Shows Requests S3 request rate, latency percentiles, errors, Iceberg operations Block storage block operations, latency, throughput and errors by protocol; unflushed data; journal fsync; chunk flushes Metadata Raft leader, term, applied index and replication lag; meta call rate, latency and errors; durable commit time Data protection degraded, at-risk and unreadable objects; when repair and scrub last ran; shards rebuilt; corrupt shards; scrub throughput Disks & OSDs OSDs up, raw capacity used; disk write, sync and read latency; per-OSD shard write latency; WAL fsync; OSD errors

Without Prometheus, the console reads the gateway's /metrics every five seconds. It computes rates and percentiles from what changed between reads, and keeps the last five minutes. With --prometheus-url set on the gateway, the longer windows (1 h to 7 d) come from Prometheus range queries. Under --no-reexport-metrics, the OSD and meta views need Prometheus, since the gateway's /metrics then no longer carries them.

docs.title: Grafana dashboards
docs.text:
deploy/monitoring/grafana/dashboards/ (and the same set in deploy/helm/objectio/dashboards/) has:

Dashboard Covers cluster-overview.json capacity, objects, request rate and latency, disk usage s3-operations.json S3 requests by operation, latency, errors, requests in flight osd-detail.json per-OSD capacity, disk health, gRPC request rate, latency (p99) and errors disk-health.json SMART readings (needs smartctl on the OSD hosts) block-storage.json block volumes, provisioned vs used, block operations, throughput, snapshots

deploy/monitoring/ also has a docker-compose Prometheus and Grafana that load these dashboards.

docs.title: Alerting
docs.text:
The metrics reference has a rule file to start from. It covers: - data safety: objects unreadable or at risk, repair not running, scrub stale, corrupt shards; - metadata: no Raft leader, repeated elections, a follower falling behind; - capacity and OSDs down; - durability latency; - block flushes failing, block read errors; - S3 server errors; - space leaking from failed shard deletes.

Data-safety alerts come first. objectio_objects_unreadable above zero, or objectio_meta_raft_has_leader at zero, needs someone now.

docs.title: Health endpoints
docs.text:
• GET /health (gateway) answers 200 {"status":"healthy"} while the process is up. It checks nothing else, so use it for liveness.
  • GET /_ready (gateway) answers 503 until meta answers and the OSDs are reachable, then 200 from then on. If some OSDs are still missing after a grace period, it becomes ready as long as enough OSDs for a write quorum are reachable. It is a startup gate for load balancers and readiness probes. It does not drop when OSDs fail later; that is what objectio_cluster_osds_up and the data-safety metrics are for.
  • GET /health on meta's and the OSDs' metrics ports answers 200 while the process is up.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: Every process logs to stderr in plain text. Set the level with --log-level (error, warn, info, debug, trace; default info). Things worth finding in logs that metrics only count: - repair work: repair: rebuilt … and repair: … needs k; - scrub results: scrub pass done: … corrupt; - shard reclaim failures, which leave space allocated; - gateway readiness, including ready without every OSD.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text: Not implemented. Requests are not traced across gateway, meta and OSD; per-phase timing of S3 PUTs and GETs is in objectio_gateway_request_phase_seconds.

docs.title: Running ObjectIO in production
docs.text: What a production cluster needs, how to size it, what to alert on, and what to do when each alert fires. Read it with the failure-recovery, meta HA, metrics and upgrades pages, which go deeper on each subject.

docs.title: Before going live
docs.text:
Every item is a default you have to change, or a requirement the software can't check for you.

Requirement Why Redundancy Set an erasure code: ec.k/ec.m in the chart (its default is k: 1, m: 0, no redundancy), or --ec-k/--ec-m. 4+2 for 6–11 hosts, 8+4 from 12. With m = 0, one lost disk loses data. Hosts At least k + m OSD hosts, one more to rebuild onto (7 for 4+2). With fewer, placement puts several shards of a stripe on one host, and losing that host can lose data. Placement doesn't refuse it. Meta 3 meta nodes (5 for two failures at once), each on its own host. Raft needs a majority: 3 survive one loss. Authentication gateway.noAuth: false in the chart (its default is true). Without it anyone who reaches the gateway can read and write everything. mTLS tls.enabled: true (mTLS). Shards and metadata cross the network between services. Drives NVMe with power-loss protection, or a UPS for the whole host. An acknowledged write is fsynced; on a drive with a volatile write cache and no PLP, a power cut can still lose it. OSD layout Shards on the raw device; each OSD's state directory (--data-dir: metadata WAL and index) on a small partition of the same drive (about 2%), not the boot disk. Every metadata write fsyncs its WAL. With 18 OSDs on a host, a shared boot disk becomes the bottleneck, and its loss takes every OSD. Clocks NTP (chrony) on every host, offset well under 100 ms. A gateway whose clock is more than 500 ms from meta's refuses writes (503) until it is back in step: write order depends on clocks. Monitoring Prometheus scraping the gateways, meta and OSDs, the alert rules loaded, and the alerts routed to someone. Repair is automatic; deciding that a host is gone for good is not. Audit gateway.audit with a system bucket, if you need an audit trail (audit). Events are spooled to disk and delivered later, so a receiver outage loses nothing.

docs.title: Capacity
docs.text:
usable ≈ raw × k / (k + m) × 0.95 − one host's worth (for rebuilds)
  • k/(k+m): 4+2 stores 1.5 bytes per byte (67% efficient), 8+4 the same, 10+4 1.4.
  • 0.95: an OSD refuses client writes past 95% of its disk (--full-ratio) and keeps the rest for repair, drain and backfill. Clients get 507 StorageFull.
  • One host's worth: when a host is lost for good, its shards are rebuilt onto the others. Keep that much free, or a host loss fills the cluster.

Worked example: 8 hosts × 18 × 7.68 TB = 1,106 TB raw. 4+2: 1,106 × 0.67 × 0.95 = 704 TB, less one host (88 TB) = about 616 TB usable.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Since B22 an OSD's memory no longer depends on how many objects it holds:

Per OSD Metadata index page cache --meta-cache-mib, 1024 by default Memtables (changes not yet checkpointed) up to 2 × 64 MiB Shard I/O buffers and the rest about 200 MB

Plan about 1.5 GB per OSD with the default cache. Per host: 18 OSDs × 1.5 GB = 27 GB, plus the gateway (2–4 GB) and the OS. 64 GB per host leaves room. A smaller cache (--meta-cache-mib 256) cuts it to about 0.7 GB per OSD, at the cost of more metadata reads from disk for objects not read recently.

Meta: plan 4–8 GB per node. Its index is in redb on disk, with a bounded cache.

docs.title: Metadata on disk
docs.text:
Each object keeps a metadata copy on each of its k + m OSDs, about 600 bytes each, plus its shard location on each OSD holding a shard:

OSD metadata per host ≈ objects_on_host × 6 copies / hosts × ~700 B

For the example above at a 1 MiB average object: about 420 million copies per host, about 300 GB, roughly 16 GB per drive. That is why the state partition is about 2% of each drive.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text: The performance page has the lab baseline. What bounds it: - Small PUTs wait for fsyncs. A drive with power-loss protection makes them cheap; one without doesn't. - Small GETs cost several internal calls each (B21 reduces them). - Large objects are bound by the network and by erasure coding: ISA-L on x86_64.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
The chart ships the rules in deploy/helm/objectio/alerts/objectio-rules.yaml: - its own Prometheus loads them when monitoring.enabled is set; - monitoring.prometheusRule.enabled also publishes them as a PrometheusRule for a prometheus-operator.

Each alert has a runbook below.

Alert Severity Runbook ObjectIOObjectsUnreadable critical Objects unreadable ObjectIOUnrecoverableStripes critical Objects unreadable ObjectIOObjectsAtRisk warning OSD down ObjectIORepairNotRunning warning Repair not running ObjectIOScrubStale warning Repair not running ObjectIOCorruptShards warning Corrupt shards ObjectIOMetaNoLeader critical Meta ObjectIOMetaElectionsChurn warning Meta ObjectIOMetaFollowerLagging warning Meta ObjectIOHealQueueFailing warning Meta ObjectIOGatewayClockSkewed critical Clock skew ObjectIOOsdDown warning OSD down ObjectIODiskNearFull warning Disks filling ObjectIODiskFull critical Disks filling ObjectIOClusterFilling warning Disks filling ObjectIOSlowShardSync warning Slow disk ObjectIOS3ServerErrors warning 5xx ObjectIOSpaceLeaking info 5xx ObjectIOAuditEventsDropped warning Audit ObjectIOReplicationLagging warning Replication ObjectIOSlowBlockJournal, ObjectIOBlockFlushFailing, ObjectIOBlockReadErrors Block

Not covered by any alert yet: certificate expiry (no metric; watch cert-manager's own), meta data-dir free space (watch with node_exporter), and the audit spool's size.

docs.title: Runbooks
docs.text: Commands are obioctl (a SigV4 client of the gateway's admin API, bin/cli/README.md in the code repo) and meta's admin port (9102).

docs.title: An OSD is down
docs.text:
What happens on its own. - Meta probes every OSD every 15 s. Three missed probes, about 45 s, mark it Down. - A Down OSD keeps its placement positions: writes go on at k + 1 shards (degraded), and reads decode around it. - Nothing is rebuilt while the OSD is merely Down. It may come back, and moving its data would cost more than waiting.

What you do. 1. obioctl node list: which OSD, and since when. 2. If the process died: restart it (systemctl restart objectio-osd, or the pod). It rejoins, and repair rebuilds only the shards written while it was gone. 3. If the host or drive is gone for good: obioctl osd set-state <node_id> out. Repair then rebuilds its shards elsewhere. Do this within a few hours: until then every stripe it held is one failure from unreadable (ObjectIOObjectsAtRisk).

Done when ObjectIOObjectsAtRisk clears and the repair counters (objectio_meta_repair_shards_rebuilt_total) stop rising.

docs.title: Replacing a disk
docs.text:
1. If the disk still reads: obioctl osd set-state <node_id> draining, and wait for obioctl cluster drain-status to show it empty. It turns out by itself.
  2. If it doesn't read: obioctl osd set-state <node_id> out.
  3. Swap the drive and start the OSD on it with the same state directory: it keeps its identity, finds the disk blank, and forgets the shards it held there.
  4. obioctl osd set-state <node_id> in. Repair rebuilds what it held.

docs.title: Disks filling or full
docs.text:
• Near full (85%). Plan capacity: add OSDs or hosts (the balancer moves data onto them), or delete data. Check obioctl cluster usage.
  • Full (95%). That OSD refuses client writes and clients get 507. The space above 95% is kept for repair. Other OSDs keep taking writes for stripes not placed on the full one.
  • Find which disks: objectio_disk_used_bytes / objectio_disk_capacity_bytes.
  • One full disk among emptier ones is uneven placement: the balancer evens it out (obioctl cluster rebalance status).
  • Everything full: add capacity. Deletes free space within a minute.
  • Don't raise --full-ratio to get writes going: it spends the room repair needs after the next failure.

docs.title: A gateway refuses writes for clock skew
docs.text:
Its clock is more than 500 ms from meta's (objectio_gateway_clock_offset_seconds gives the offset). Writes through it fail with 503 (clients retry, ideally through another gateway). Reads work.

Fix time sync on that host (chronyc tracking, chronyc makestep). Writes resume within a second of the clock coming back in step. Don't restart the gateway: it doesn't help.

docs.title: Meta has no leader, or elects often
docs.text:
• No leader for more than a minute: fewer than a majority of meta nodes are up or can reach each other. Writes fail with 503; reads of object data mostly still work.
  • curl http://<meta>:9102/status on each node shows its role, its term, and who it thinks leads.
  • Bring a majority back. A node lost for good is replaced with POST :9102/add-learner then POST :9102/change-membership (meta HA).
  • No procedure exists yet for a majority lost for good.
  • Elections churn: usually a node that drops off the network intermittently, or a disk too slow for its heartbeats. Compare the nodes' objectio_meta_commit_seconds.
  • A follower lags: it is catching up, or its disk is slow. One far behind is sent a snapshot.
  • Heal queue failing: writes reached a quorum of metadata copies while meta was unreachable; gateways retry queuing them for 10 minutes. Persistent failures mean meta is down: see above.

docs.title: Repair not running
docs.text:
objectio_meta_repair_last_pass_timestamp_seconds hasn't moved in three repair intervals (--repair-interval-secs, an hour by default). Repair runs on the meta leader: - check that there is one (above); - check the leader's log for repair: lines; - a pass that never ends is usually a target OSD that accepts connections but doesn't answer.

Scrub stale: an OSD hasn't finished a scrub pass in 8 days. Check that OSD's log; a pass on a very full disk at 50 MiB/s (--scrub-rate-mib) can take days.

docs.title: Corrupt shards
docs.text: Scrub or a read found shards that don't match their checksums. The OSD reports them, and repair rebuilds them from the rest of the stripe. If the count keeps rising on one OSD, its drive is failing: check its SMART metrics (objectio_disk_smart_*) and replace it (above).

docs.title: Objects unreadable or unrecoverable
docs.text: Some stripes have fewer than k good shards: more failures at once than the code tolerates. 1. Bring back every OSD that is down but intact (powered off, network). Their shards make the stripes readable again. 2. Don't set OSDs out or wipe disks until this is resolved. 3. What can't be brought back is lost. No tool yet lists which objects are affected.

docs.title: A slow disk
docs.text: p99 shard fsync over 100 ms. Find the OSD from the per-OSD objectio_osd_disk_seconds. A drive getting slower often fails next: check SMART, and drain it (replacing a disk) if it doesn't recover. A drive without power-loss protection is always slow to fsync.

docs.title: S3 requests failing with 5xx
docs.text:
• 503s during a fault are expected: clients retry.
  • Persistent 503s mean meta has no leader, OSDs are unreachable, or a gateway refuses writes for clock skew. See those runbooks.
  • A 500 is a bug: report it with the gateway's log line for the request id.

Space leaking: shard deletes are failing, so freed space stays allocated until a later repair pass. It is usually an OSD that is down. A leak is never a loss.

docs.title: Audit events dropped
docs.text:
Events are spooled on the gateway's disk until delivered. Drops mean: - the spool filled (--audit-spool-max-bytes) because a receiver has been down for long; or - a gateway pod was deleted without a clean shutdown.

Fix the receiver; size the spool for the longest outage you accept (audit).

docs.title: Replication lagging
docs.text: The oldest unreplicated version is over an hour old. That is how much a loss of this site would lose. Check the target's reachability and credentials, and the result="error" count of objectio_replication_sent_total (replication).

docs.title: Block volumes
docs.text:
The block gateway journals writes on its own disk before storing them as chunks. - Slow journal fsync: slows every block write. - Flush failing: chunks aren't being stored; the write cache fills and writes stall. - Read errors: reads that couldn't be served.

The journal is a single copy on the block gateway's disk: losing that disk loses writes not yet flushed (a known gap; see the block design).

docs.title: Certificates expiring
docs.text: cert-manager renews 30 days before expiry. The services read their certificates only at start, so after a renewal restart them (rolling): kubectl rollout restart statefulset/<release>-meta statefulset/<release>-osd deployment/<release>-gateway. An expired certificate stops every internal call. There is no expiry metric yet: alert on cert-manager's certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text: Follow upgrades: meta first, then OSDs, then gateways, one at a time. Then obioctl upgrade status, and obioctl upgrade finalize once every node runs the new release. Back up meta.redb from a stopped follower first.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text: Move a cluster to the next release one node at a time, under traffic. Design: core/upgrade-path.md.

docs.title: What to know first
docs.text:
• One release at a time. Go from each release to the next; to skip releases, upgrade through each in turn.
  • Format levels. Each release has a format level. During an upgrade, nodes on the new release read what it introduces but keep writing the previous release's formats, so you can still go back. The new formats start only when you finalize.
  • No going back after finalize. Back up meta first (stop a meta follower and copy its meta.redb; an export command is planned).
  • Too-old nodes are refused. After finalize, meta refuses any node or client from an older release, and a node too old for the cluster stops at start-up with a message saying so, instead of running and misreading data.

docs.title: The procedure
docs.text:
1. Back up meta.
  2. Meta nodes: the followers one at a time, then the leader. After each, wait until it has rejoined (GET /status on its admin port shows it with the others' last_applied).
  3. OSDs, one failure domain at a time. After each, wait until it is registered and healthy (obioctl node list). A restart needs no drain: reads tolerate up to m missing shards meanwhile.
  4. Gateways and block gateways, in any order.
  5. Check that every node runs the new release:
obioctl upgrade status

It lists every node heard from in the last 90 seconds, with its release and format level, and says what blocks finalizing: a meta node or an OSD that hasn't reported (down, or still on a release from before format levels), or a node still on the old release. Gateways are stateless and can't be listed in advance, so check that every gateway you run appears.

  1. Finalize:
obioctl upgrade finalize

It is refused while anything blocks it.

To go back before step 6, run the same steps in reverse order with the previous release's binaries.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: Roll the meta and OSD StatefulSets one pod at a time (partition), each gated on readiness, in the order above, then run obioctl upgrade finalize.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Both calls are system admin only.

Call GET /_admin/upgrade active_level, finalize_to, can_finalize, blockers, and nodes (kind, id, release, format level, address, seconds since last report) POST /_admin/upgrade/finalize Raises the active level. Returns 409 with the blockers when not every node is ready

docs.title: Clusters from before format levels
docs.text: Releases v0.4.0 and earlier can't be upgraded: install the new release fresh and copy the data across (with bucket replication, or any S3 tool).
